News.title: Several dead after horror crash between car and police vehicle on major A-road in early hours
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SMASH TRAGEDY Several dead after horror crash between car and police vehicle on major A-road in early hours

MULTIPLE people have died after a crash involving a police vehicle and another car in the early hours.

Emergency services rushed to the A66 in South Bank, Cleveland at 3.40am this morning and a significant number remain on the scene.

The collision involved a police car and a Volkswagen Passat and resulted in several fatalities, police said.

The road will remain closed for some time the force added.





A spokesperson for Cleveland Police said: “Around 3:39am this morning, a collision took place involving a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank.

“Sadly, the collision has resulted in multiple fatalities.

“There are significant emergency vehicles on the scene, and the road will remain closed for some time.

“The public are asked to use alternative routes.



“We are working to identify the victims and contact their families.

“This is a quickly evolving incident and we ask that members of the public respectfully avoid speculation.”

A spokesperson for Cleveland Fire Brigade added: “Cleveland Fire Brigade is currently attending a road traffic collision on the westbound carriageway of the A66 South Bank area. Please avoid the area if you can.”

News.title: Is THIS Putin’s next land grab? Tyrant fires missiles off Pacific islands in ‘alarming’ escalation over naval flashpoint
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin has launched a missile test off a group of disputed Japanese Islands, in an “alarming” escalation that could spark a global conflict.

The tests, which come off the back of Putin’s first visit to the contested Kuril islands, marks a “direct escalation” against Japan, experts warn.



Missiles were reportedly fired in a simulation of an attack on enemy vessels, hitting targets located 186 miles away, Russia’s Pacific fleet said.

A unit equipped with a surface-to-ship missile system conducted the live test, alongside a guided missile cruiser and a nuclear-powered submarine.





Professor James Brown, of Temple University in Japan, told The Sun: “Russia is trying to prove its undiminished military power in the far east despite enormous losses in Ukraine.

“But this is a very tense region. Wherever you look there are flashpoints and they’re getting worse.

“It could be a World War One situation – where a minor flashpoint triggers a global conflict.”

A long-standing security tinderbox, the four southern-most Kuril islands were seized from Japan by the Soviet Union at the end of the Second World War.



An estimated 17,000 Japanese residents were subsequently expelled from the territory which Russia now controls.



But Japan maintains territorial rights over of the chain, which it calls the Northern Territories, and argues they are illegally occupied.

The decade-long dispute has kept the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.

But their competing sovereignty have become entangled in a much wider contest.

It comes just weeks after Putin made his first high-profile visit to the island group.

The tyrant arrived in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the Far Eastern island’s administrative centre on August 4, to participate in the final stage of a war exercise conducted by the Pacific Fleet.



In his address to Russian servicemen, Putin said exercises are necessary to maintain readiness and protect his country’s interests and security in the region.

But Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi condemned the visit.

He said: “The Northern Territories, including Iturup Island, are inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit.”



Over the years Russia has beefed up its military presence on the islands in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance to not let go of the territory.

The Kurils give Moscow a strategic foothold in the Pacific.

The islands also have a practical value neighbouring key maritime routes, while nearby Sakhalin has substantial oil and gas resources.

Moscow has also been conducting military activities with China and North Korea, including joint bomber flights and naval drills.



This month, North Korea launched a string of missiles towards the Sea of Japan, while the region has also seen a rise in joint air and maritime patrols by Moscow and Beijing.

It has fuelled concerns about an emerging anti-Western alignment involving the power trio.

Experts say this is only the start of military activity in the area as tensions spiral out of control.

James said: “You’ve got North Korea testing ballistic missiles, China’s claims to Taiwan.

“At the least we will see more flights by nuclear capable bombers and more infringements within countries claimed airspace.



“But there could also be more serious incidents like targeting of other countries vessels.”

A direct confrontation like this could see the regional tensions explode in just “moments”, James said.

He added: “You have Russian fighter jets and Chinese fighter jets operating in this area.

“If that provoked another country to retaliate with fire things can escalate very very quickly.

“It would be a World War One situation – where a minor flashpoint triggers a global conflict.



“The US would be dragged in, China could lean on Russia and you also have North and South Korea getting involved.”

It comes just weeks after Putin accused ⁠Nato of ⁠infiltrating the ⁠Asia-Pacific region, and ​creating ⁠tension in ‌the Arctic.

He went on to accuse Japan of imposing sanctions on Russia that he said were “unprovoked” on Russia’s part.

European security expert Anthony Glees told The Sun: “Putin is undoubtedly ramping up the pressure on Japan.

“He’s doing this whilst Xi flexes his imperialist muscle in South China sea and Kim Jong-un launches missiles in the Sea of Japan, literally over the heads of the Japanese.



“This Russian exercise is a big worry for all of the democratic Asia-Pacific nations, as well as for us here in Europe.”

Glees said the move forms part of an “alarming” challenge by the three strong-men to challenge the West in the Asia-Pacific.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “Putin and Xi are major landgrabbers – as Ukraine, Taiwan and the newly built island bases in the South China Sea show.

“Putin is warning that the whole region could fall victim to the imperial designs of this new triple Axis of Evil.”

News.title: Cops scrambled to Manchester Airport after person ‘gets onto airfield’ – as seven flights diverted and 17 held in air
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAVEL CHAOS Cops scrambled to Manchester Airport after person ‘gets onto airfield’ – as seven flights diverted and 17 held in air

A MAJOR airport was forced to divert seven flights after an individual reportedly got onto the airfield prompting mayhem.

At least 17 planes were held in the sky at Manchester Airport after the person breached security by entering the prohibited space.



The airport was plunged into chaos after the incident, prompting a quick emergency response.

An individual was arrested at the scene after around 15 minutes, and has since been taken to hospital.



One flight from Cape Verde had to be diverted to East Midland Airport because of the incident.

Another flight arriving from Morocco was redirected to Birmingham Airport.



The airport has reportedly since gone back to normal and a temporary fix has been put in place.

A spokesperson for Manchester Airport said: “A person encroached onto the airfield shortly before midnight last night. They were quickly apprehended by staff and arrested by Greater Manchester Police.

“The airfield was closed for around 15 minutes while the incident was handled and the breach was repaired. That resulted in 7 diverted flights and 17 delayed flights.”

Greater Manchester Police has been contacted for comment.

News.title: At least 5 killed as ‘speeding’ bus slams into crowd after ‘driver lost control’ while trying to avoid crash with truck
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

DEADLY SMASH At least 5 killed as ‘speeding’ bus slams into crowd after ‘driver lost control’ while trying to avoid crash with truck

AT least five people have been killed and five injured as a bus ploughed into a crowd watching an orchestra performance.

The bus reportedly slammed into the crowd at high speed after its driver lost control while trying to avoid a head-on collision with a truck.



Cops said the bus driver fled the scene.

The horror unfolded at 10.45pm on Friday night in Lauriya, northern India.



A huge crowd had spilled out onto the roadside to watch a concert in Bihar’s West Champaran district.

The concert had been organised as part of a ceremony to celebrate a newborn baby in the village.

Police said: “Suddenly, a speeding bus en route to Bettiah from Gorakhpur lost control and ploughed into the gathering.”

Witnesses said a truck carrying gas cylinders was driving in the opposite direction.

The bus swerved to avoid the truck and smashed into the gathered crowd instead, police said.

After smashing into the crowd, police said the bus driver sped away from the scene.



The driver later abandoned the bus, which was seized by cops, they told the Hindustan Times.

Narkatiyaganj police officer Ajay Prakash Singh told PTI news: “While trying to avert a head-on collision with a truck, the bus ploughed into a crowd attending a cultural event on the roadside, killing five men and injuring several others.”

Two people died at the scene and three more in hospital.

They were named by police as Sanjay Mahto, Bhola Dubey, Bahadur Mahto, Devendra Dubey, and Changur Ram.

Five others remain in hospital.



Police have launched an investigation into the incident.

They are considering speeding as a potential cause of the deadly smash.

It comes after at least eight people were killed and another ten injured after a bus plunged off a mountain road in northern India earlier this month.

The bus suddenly veered off the edge of a cliff and flipped over – trapping passengers inside.

The victims included the driver and the conductor.

News.title: My dog is going BLIND and may need her eyeballs removed after eating pet food recalled across UK – it’s ruined our lives
News.content:
A DOG owner has been left devastated as her cockapoo is going blind after eating a popular dog food.

The owner claims the food has been blinding her pet in a “months long” ordeal as the company issues a voluntary recall on its meals.



Carolyn Groombridge, from Hertfordshire, claims her dog has been suffering from increasingly severe eye problems – and is even going blind – after being fed Years premium dog food for more than a year.

Kiki, the five-year-old mini schnoodle, began showing symptoms of what Carolyn initially believed was an infection, after noticing “gunk” and “discharge” coming from her eyes.



Following weeks of unsuccessful antibiotic and steroid treatments, vets urged Carolyn to take her pet in for a specialist diagnosis at The Royal Veterinary College (RVC) in Hertfordshire, where they told her that “Kiki was at risk of losing both her eyes”.

Carolyn said: “The vets even said she could have her eyes removed, but I couldn’t do that to her.”



After diagnosing Kiki with absolute keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye) in both eyes and stromal ulcers (open sores) in her left eye, Carolyn claims the ordeal has “ruined our lives”.

“She’s a member of our family and it’s just horrible seeing her suffer like this.”



But despite vets spending months investigating what could cause the pup’s tear ducts to stop functioning entirely, it was only this week that the pieces fell into place.

“On Monday night, at 10:30pm, I received an email from Years saying ‘do not feed your dog this food anymore’,” Carolyn said.

Years – a premium subscription-based company specialising in fresh dog food, notified its 40,000 customers earlier this week that it would be voluntarily recalling all Years Fresh Meals (excluding the Chef’s Collection).



This was after its buckwheat-based meals were found to be linked with potentially causing eye problems in dogs.

A day later (August 18), a Years spokesperson confirmed to The Sun that 192 customers in total reported potential, as yet unverified, eye issues in their pets.

The brand added that it has now launched a formal investigation into its signature meals, in collaboration with customers and veterinary professionals, and is reformulating products to remove buckwheat.

The news, Carolyn said, was devastating.

“I’ve been feeding her this everyday, effectively continuing to poison her while I’ve been giving her medication.”



“I spent so much time researching a decent food and ensuring Kiki gets all the right nutrients, only to find out that it’s actually the food that has been causing her problems.”

The family tried contacting the dog food brand as soon as Carolyn received the email, but said they have yet to receive a reply.

Vets at the RVC told Carolyn they had never seen a case “so bad” before, and had ruled out a genetic condition as it would take years to develop to this level of severity.

Instead, the practitioners believe Kiki’s problems may be the result of an immune response which has attacked her tear glands – rendering them completely dry.

Now, more than two and a half months after Kiki first experienced symptoms, Carolyn fears the condition is “irreversible”.



Despite giving her medication which requires drops every two hours, day and night, to stop her from getting ulcers that might damage her eyes even more, the family has seen no improvement.

“She looks worse than ever; her eyes don’t even open anymore and if you try to peel them open, they’re swollen and red.”

“She’s normally such a happy fun-loving dog, everyone who sees her loves her.”

With Kiki’s sight damaged from scarring on her corneas, her family wants compensation from the company to help put towards the pet’s £200 medication and rising vet costs.

“The heartbreaking thing is that Kiki loved their food before all this, their customer service had always been great,” explains Carolyn.



Years previously told The Sun that “several findings” had led it to investigate buckwheat as a potential contributing factor, including timing, with all confirmed cases emerging after buckwheat was introduced into the recipe.

It also noted there could be potential supply contamination, with possible contamination identified in supplier product during its investigation.

The brand added that buckwheat was a common approved ingredient used across many pet foods, and had gone through a “thorough process” before being introduced in its meals.

A Years spokesperson told The Sun: “Years exists for one reason: to give people more time with their dogs, and the reports we have received are deeply upsetting to everyone here.

“As a result of the reports, we took the step to voluntarily recall our fresh meals because, while the evidence is still developing, we are not prepared to take chances with the dogs people trust us to feed.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Our investigation is currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply, rather than buckwheat itself, although a definitive cause has not yet been established.

“Independent laboratory testing is underway, alongside our wider investigation, to understand exactly what has happened. We want to give customers clear, evidence-based answers rather than speculate while that work continues, and we will communicate the findings as soon as the investigation is complete.”

News.title: Urgent hunt to find missing woman last seen entering taxi with suitcase and travelling to UK city
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIND HER Urgent hunt to find missing woman last seen entering taxi with suitcase and travelling to UK city

A woman has been missing for three days after she was last seen getting into a taxi with a suitcase.

Marie vanished from Workington on the evening of August 18 and police have urged anyone who sees her to call 999.

She was last seen entering a taxi which officers believe took her to Carlisle.

Marie has long, dark brown hair and is believed to be wearing a green coat or jacket with baggy jeans.





She is said to be carrying a Morrison’s bag for life and a suitcase.

Cumbria Police is concerned for her welfare and urged any witnesses to come forward.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Have you seen missing person Marie Conaghan?

“Marie is missing from Workington and was last seen entering a taxi between 5pm and 6pm on the 18 August 2026.

“It is believed the taxi has travelled to Carlisle.”

“Marie has long, dark, brown hair. She is believed to be wearing a green coat/jacket, baggy jeans and carrying a black rucksack, multicoloured Morrison’s bag for life and a suitcase.

“She is believed to be in Carlisle.

“Officers are concerned for Marie’s welfare and are encouraging anyone who can help find her to come forward.



“If you see Marie, please call 999.”

News.title: Boy who was ‘raised by wolves’ & spent 12 years living like an animal with pack dies aged 80
News.content:
FINAL HOWL Boy who was ‘raised by wolves’ & spent 12 years living like an animal with pack dies aged 80

A MAN who claimed to have been raised by wolves has died aged 80.

Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja, the so-called “Mowgli of Spain“, had been completely isolated from human society since the age of seven.



The Civil Guard discovered the youngster, then aged 19, prowling across the Sierra Morena mountain range on all fours, barefoot and half-naked.

Grunting in response to questions and with thick callouses on his hands and feet, shocked officers wondered how he had survived so long in the wilderness.



He later claimed that a mother wolf taught him how to find berries and mushrooms to eat – and even flung him hunks of meat to survive.

Marcos, who lived in the northern Spanish province of Ourense, passed away on August 15, aged 80.

Born in 1946, Marcos’s mother died when he was only three years old – and when his father remarried he was allegedly abused by his stepmother.

Living in poverty, his father sent – or possibly sold – him to work for a goatherder in the mountains.

But when the older man suddenly passed away he left Marcos, then aged around seven, to fend for himself.

He recalled how he was cared for by a she-wolf, saying: “After feeding her pups, she threw me a piece of meat.



“I took it, ate it, and thought she was going to bite me, but she put her tongue out and started to lick me. After that, I was one of the family.”

The young Spaniard also had a pet snake who he fed with goat’s milk – but was eventually discovered by the Civil Guard in 1965.

Cops were forced to bind and gag him because he kept biting officers.



When his father – who was never charged with child abuse – saw him again, his only comment was to say that his son had lost his jacket.

Following his “rescue” by the Civil Guard, Marcos struggled to adapt to modern life.

In a 2018 interview, he said he loved animals more than humans and that “the happiest days of my life” had been spent in the wilderness.

“I could not cope with so much noise, the cars, and people going back and forwards like ants”, he told the BBC.

“But at least ants all go in the same direction. People went everywhere. I was scared of crossing the road.”



He added that people laughed at him because he didn’t understand football or modern politics.

Working was also difficult because colleagues took advantage of his naivety to swindle him out of money.

Trying to return to his childhood wolf pack was impossible however.



Speaking to El Pais he said: “You can tell that they are right there, you hear them panting, it gives you goosebumps … but it’s not that easy to see them.

“There are wolves and if I call out to them they are going to respond, but they are not going to approach me,

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I smell like people, I wear cologne.”

His story sparked worldwide interest – with PHD thesis being written about his life as well as a 2010 film called Among Wolves.

News.title: Fury over Labour’s plans to stop criminals jailed for manslaughter being freed early but other killers set to walk free
News.content:
CAMPAIGNERS have reacted with fury over plans to bar some criminals convicted of manslaughter from early release while other dangerous killers are still set to walk free.

The Prime Minister is believed to be considering removing unlawful manslaughter from the planned jail reforms in order to stop PC Andrew Harper’s killers from getting out early.



But it means that criminals convicted of more serious offences, such as voluntary manslaughter, will still benefit from less time behind bars.

A review of the scheme, which will see some lags spend just a third or half of their terms in prison, will be presented to parliament in a fortnight.



Victims rights campaigner Hetti Barkworth-Nanton CBE has written to the Lord Chancellor to urge him not to take a “piecemeal” approach to the justice system.

Her best friend Joanna Simpson was killed by her estranged husband Robert Brown who was later convicted of voluntary manslaughter with diminished responsibility.

In the letter, seen by The Sun, she wrote: “Whilst I wouldn’t question the horror of the killing of PC Harper, killed horrifically whilst attending an incident, taking this sort of piecemeal approach specifically to prevent certain killers from being released is an insult to so many other victims.

“Specifically when looking at different categories of manslaughter, the most serious form of manslaughter is voluntary manslaughter – in all but name murder with a mitigating factor that changes the conviction to manslaughter.



“These types of manslaughter are hard enough for victims to accept at the best of times, but if you announce an exemption for one type of involuntary manslaughter without including voluntary manslaughter it would honestly be a disgrace.

“I urge you to reconsider if indeed what is reported by the media this morning is the direction you are intending to go in.

“We must drive exemptions based on seriousness of the crime not based on one particular case.”

Involuntary manslaughter, which is what Bowers and Cole were convicted of, is unlawful killing without the intent to kill or cause really serious harm.

There are two classes of involuntary manslaughter: unlawful act manslaughter, when someone is killed due to a criminal act, and manslaughter by gross negligence, when someone dies due to a breach of care.



Voluntary manslaughter occurs when all the elements for murder are present, including an intention to kill or cause really serious harm, but the crime is reduced to manslaughter by reason of loss of control or diminished responsibility.

Jo Earley, CEO of charity Support After Murder and Manslaughter said: “Whilst we welcome consideration of exempting unlawful act manslaughter, we urge the Government to go further and exclude all manslaughter convictions from the early release scheme.

“There can be a fine line between murder and manslaughter, and offenders convicted of manslaughter may still pose a significant risk to the public.



“The early release of an offender can be devastating and feel like a complete injustice. We must place the rights, needs and views of bereaved families at the heart of any decision about an offender’s release.

“They should not be made to feel that the person responsible for their loved one’s death is being prioritised over their right to safety and justice.”

Frank Malone from Advocacy After Fatal Domestic Abuse told The Sun: “Government’s first duty is to protect its citizens. So, we have to expect that governments will develop prison policy in a systematic way.

“Any other approach, i.e., an ad hoc one, not only ignores many victims and their families, it undermines public protection.”

Lord Thomas, an independent crossbench peer who previously served as lord chief justice of England and Wales, said “it may not be that straightforward” for prison staff to determine which type of manslaughter an inmate committed from their prison records.



But, he said, it “should be relatively easy to tell that from the sentencing remarks, which are always transmitted with the prisoner’s record”.

Asked this week about the proposals to exclude certain manslaughter cases, Burnham told reporters: “At this moment in time, this is speculation.”

He said: “I’ve said I want to do everything possible to ensure we don’t see the release of people involved in the killing of Pc Harper and other individuals.

“I recognise that it’s very hard for his family. The anniversary of his death passed just at the weekend, so we understand that this is a difficult time.

“But it is important, given the public concern, that I do everything possible to get this right. That I do everything possible to minimise early release. That’s why we’re looking at every way I can do that, with the Justice Secretary, and we’ll present our findings in two weeks’ time.”



A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We have always stated we wanted to go further, and we are fast-tracking a plan to keep more of the most dangerous offenders behind bars.

“That’s on top of murderers and those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences who are already blocked from any changes.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Robert Buckland, a former Tory Justice Secretary, said: “Tinkering with this deeply flawed early release scheme to exempt only some killers from it will create further injustices and insults to the families of the victims.

“The government should scrap this scheme and start again.”

News.title: Multiple deaths after collision between police vehicle and car
News.content:
Multiple people have died in a crash involving a police vehicle and a car, police have said.

The collision involved a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough in Teesside, at about 03:39 BST, Cleveland Police said.

A spokesman for the force said: "Sadly, the collision has resulted in multiple fatalities.

"We are working to identify the victims and contact their families."

The road remains closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane and the force said it would do so "for some time".

It said there were still "significant emergency service vehicles" on the scene.

News.title: Girl, 6, dies days after Shoreham sea tragedy killed three family members
News.content:
A six-year-old girl has died in hospital after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex, in an incident which also killed her father, mother and sister.

Saja El-Khawas, a British Palestinian from London, was pulled from the sea by emergency crews on Tuesday.

Her father Hassan El-Khawas, 55, mother Zeina Alayn, 37, and 14-year-old sister Sara, died despite the efforts of paramedics at the scene.

Emergency services were called to the sea off Shoreham Fort at about 14:40 BST on Tuesday to a report of four people in difficulty in the water.

News.title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
News.content:
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than at any point in the last nine years, new data shows.

Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.

In 2017, it was closer to one in five.

The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.

Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.

For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.

Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.

News.title: Sydney Marathon medal mistakenly depicts Munich stadium
News.content:
One week out from the world-renowned Sydney Marathon, organisers face questions about whether designers etched the wrong city's stadium on the participation medal.

The medal appears to feature a stadium carved in the likeness of Allianz Arena in the German city of Munich, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney â which the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course runs past.

The BBC has reached out to Sydney Marathon for comment.

Some 40,000 runners will be taking part in the event on 30 August, after more than 120,000 ballot entries.

Speculation about a possible mix-up began after Sydney Marathon's official social media account unveiled its design for the 2026 medal, inviting users to "look closely and you'll find the story of the course in the details".

They continued: "A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way - starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House."

News.title: How this 1960s ex-council house is managing to stay cool without air con
News.content:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes, external in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house with no air-conditioning is managing to beat the heat.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.

News.title: As they return to the UK, Harry and Meghan search for a brand that sticks
News.content:
In late July, the Duchess of Sussex's lifestyle range, called As ever, launched a "rich, vibrant" blackberry spread alongside a softly lit video of her picking the fruit.

A month later, Meghan and her husband Prince Harry are returning to live in the UK just as blackberry season ends. Perhaps we can expect another video soon, shot on these shores.

Or perhaps not, because experts say the Harry and Meghan brand is at a crossroads.

After the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's acrimonious exit from the Royal Family in 2020, the projects marking their fresh start in California - from streaming to signature scents - have mostly failed to find large audiences, and experts say it's unclear where the couple goes from here.

Their return to the UK has surprised many and we don't know their reasons for the switch, but what's clear is that they will not be working royals when they return. So what could they be doing instead?

News.title: GTA 6 leaks - a nightmare or a blip for the biggest video game of the year?
News.content:
Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

News.title: Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction
News.content:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

News.title: Advisor O'Neill rules out government job but backs PM's devolution plans
News.content:
The economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer, was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, he said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

"I've decided to not take a formal role," he said.

"It's not because of any policy disagreements. I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

"I'll continue to, hopefully, maintain an informal relationship with the PM and his team," he added.

He said he did not want "the constraints of a blind trust and all the constraints that would be necessary".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Brief break from rain as sunshine returns for weekend
News.content:
After the spell of showery weather earlier this week, a strong area of high pressure is set to bring bright and sunny weather to much of the UK this weekend.

Daytime temperatures will feel pleasantly warm - though a long way off from the record heat experienced earlier this month.

Nights are expected to be mostly clear, leading to a significant temperature contrast from morning lows to afternoon highs.

While Saturday and Sunday will bring a brief break from the rain for many, unsettled weather will return early next week.

News.title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.

Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.

The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.

The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.

Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.

Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.

News.title: Murder probe after wildfire uncovers body in park
News.content:
A murder investigation is under way after human bones were uncovered at a west London park following a wildfire, the Metropolitan Police said.

Emergency services were called to Bedfont Pits in Hounslow at about 18:35 BST on Wednesday, 12 August.

A police spokesperson said the remains were found by a member of the public after the wildfire affected an area of woodland known as The Pits.

Following a post-mortem examination, police said the bones belonged to a woman aged between 25 and 45. They said it was not clear how long the remains had been there and officers were still working to identify her.

News.title: Arran ferry evacuated over 'bomb threat' by passenger rescued from sea
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has been arrested after a ferry service on Scotland's west coast was evacuated over a bomb threat.

Operator CalMac said a passenger was reported overboard on the MV Caledonian Isles 16:40 service, carrying 329 people from Brodick on the Isle of Arran.

The BBC understands that after being pulled from the sea by the ferry's rescue boat, the man then told crew that there was a bomb on board.

All passengers were removed on foot at Ardrossan so the vessel could be searched. Police Scotland said it was established that the threats "were not credible".

The passengers and others waiting at the port were taken to a nearby supermarket car park by police while the search was carried out.

After this was complete, officers allowed people back on board to collect their vehicles.

News.title: Teen blinded by firework wants ban on public sales
News.content:
A teenager blinded by a firework on Bonfire Night has called for a ban on them being sold to the public.

Tom Parnaby was 18 when he and a friend were badly injured in the accident on 5 November 2025.

He is now campaigning for more controlled firework displays and tighter regulations on sales.

Tom, who has since become a father for the first time, said despite what happened to him he does not hate fireworks, but thinks the "public sale of them is crazy".

Tom suffered injuries to his face leading to him losing his sight during an incident with friends on the beach in Scarborough, North Yorkshire.

The teenager said focusing on the baby daughter who he would never be able to see had helped him pull through.

"I am just grateful to have her with me," he said.

"It is a lot easier to focus on what's coming than what's behind with her there."

News.title: Man tracks down siblings who sent him Christmas present as he fled war 33 years ago
News.content:
A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more than 30 years ago.

Dalibor Sentic was 10 when in the early 1990s his family fled the newly independent country - which had recently become involved in the Balkan war - for Stockholm, Sweden.

Dalibor had received a gift from two young siblings, eight-year-old Claire and Peter, six, from Mold, Flintshire, and had hoped to track them down but only had limited information on them.

Decades later, Dalibor, now 44, was able to find the pair to thank them, saying the gesture had "meant a lot" at a time of great difficulty.

Describing fleeing his homeland as a child, Dalibor said "we had basically nothing".

"It was like starting all over again.

"I was so innocent but remember hearing the bombs," he said.

Dalibor said that, despite the conflict surrounding them, his parents made sure he felt "loved and secure", although he added that moving countries was "tough on a kid".

Some months before they fled, Dalibor said his teacher took him into a room full of packages, telling him to choose one to open.

It contained a picture of Claire and Peter, which he held onto for more than three decades.

"The older you get the more you understand the meaning behind small gestures... it meant a lot," he said.

News.title: Prince Harry and six others face privacy case legal bill of up to £34.5m
News.content:
Prince Harry and six other public figures face paying up to Â£34.5m to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional order for legal costs over their failed privacy case.

The seven claimants, also including Sir Elton John and Liz Hurley, must pay an initial Â£9.54m by Friday of next week to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL).

The judge ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before trial, criticising how they presented their claims as "unreasonable to a high degree".

On 7 July, Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the claims of unlawful information-gathering, which ANL denied.

The Duke of Sussex and the other six claimants have until 2 October to attempt to launch an appeal.

Those other claimants are Sir Elton John and his husband David Furnish, former Liberal Democrat deputy leader Sir Simon Hughes, racial justice campaigner Baroness Lawrence, and actresses Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley,

They had insurance to cover up to Â£16.2m of Association Newspapers' costs in the event of losing the case - but Friday's ruling means the newspaper group could now try to recover up to the Â£34.5m that it said it had to spend to defend itself. This means the duke and others could face a bill of some Â£18m.

Justice Nicklin said: "I regard a claim for costs in excess of Â£34 million as, on its face, excessive and as giving rise to real concerns as to whether all of the costs now claimed by Associated were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount."

But he added he had "decided not to impose a ceiling on Associated's recoverable costs", as it would "be too broad-brushed, would risk unfairness, and would be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary".

The judge also ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, which is more favourable to the publisher in terms of the amount it can recover, aside from where orders had already been made.

He added it was "striking" that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group of seven claimants.

He said: "That matters. Serious allegations of criminality or grave impropriety cannot properly be left hanging over individuals in that way.

"If a party no longer advances such an allegation, or no longer has a proper evidential basis for advancing it, the allegation should be withdrawn clearly and in terms.

Fewer than one in five women in England now take folic acid before pregnancy. This is down from one in four just five years ago.

The decline is worrying because it could undermine the progress that has been made in recent years to prevent serious birth defects linked to low folic acid intake.

Although the UK government has mandated that from December 2026 all non-wholemeal wheat flour must be fortified with folic acid, the amount being added isn’t enough to stop the ongoing need for folic acid supplements.

As such, all women planning to become pregnant should still take a folic acid supplement daily when trying to get pregnant and during their first trimester.

Folic acid is the synthetic form of folate (also known as vitamin B9). It helps cells grow and divide.

In early pregnancy, folic acid supports the development of the neural tube, which becomes the baby’s brain and spinal cord. If the tube does not close properly, babies can develop conditions such as spina bifida or anencephaly.

open image in gallery Folic acid is being added to non-wholemeal wheat flour across the UK ( Getty/iStock )

Spina bifida happens when a baby’s spine and spinal cord do not fully develop, while anencephaly is a severe condition where major parts of the brain and skull are absent.

In England, it’s estimated that some form of neural tube defect occurs in 12.5 per 100,000 births. Most of these conditions can be prevented if a woman has enough folate before becoming pregnant. Other factors, such as not getting enough vitamin B12, may also play a role. Mild forms affect 5 to 10 million people.

Neural tube defects can also lead to pregnancy loss, death soon after birth or lifelong disability, with devastating impacts on families.

Because these conditions develop so early in pregnancy, taking a folic acid supplement before getting pregnant remains one of the most important ways to reduce the risk.

A widening gap

The decline in folic acid use before pregnancy is worrying for a number of reasons.

Uptake is already low in certain groups, with data showing supplement use is consistently lowest among Black and Asian women and those living in deprived areas.

About the authors Danielle Schoenaker is an Associate Professor of Preconception Health and Care at the University of Southampton. Keith Godfrey is a Professor of Epidemiology and Human Development at the University of Southampton. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Uptake has also fallen steeply in the north-east of England and remains well below the national average in the west midlands. These differences show folic acid supplement use is not simply individual choice.

Several factors influence uptake. Some women are not planning a pregnancy, while others do not know when folic acid is needed, believe a healthy diet is enough, or lack access to pre-pregnancy care.

Previous pregnancy experience does not necessarily help, either. Research suggests women who have been pregnant before are less likely to take folic acid during their next pregnancy compared to first-time mothers. Possible reasons for this include unplanned later pregnancies, competing childcare responsibilities and a lower sense of need after a prior healthy pregnancy. So knowledge is not enough.

It’s currently not clear why supplement use has been declining overall. It may reflect a combination of limited and unequal access to timely pre-pregnancy advice or practical barriers such as cost and availability. It could also be due to confusion about whether flour fortification means supplements are no longer needed.

Why fortification isn’t enough

open image in gallery It’s important that women take a folic acid supplement before becoming pregnant, and during the first 12 weeks ( Getty/iStock )

The key challenge with folic acid is timing. The neural tube closes by about four weeks after conception, often before a woman knows she is pregnant.

As many pregnancies are unplanned, this means many women will not start supplements before the neural tube closes. Even those intending to become pregnant may miss this critical window if they do not receive timely advice.

So relying on supplements alone to prevent serious birth defects is not a good strategy.

Mandatory fortification is valuable because it does not depend on pregnancy planning. It safely raises folate levels across the population, including in women not taking supplements or who become pregnant unexpectedly.

Countries which have already introduced mandatory fortification – including the US, Canada, Chile and Australia – show how powerful this can be in preventing neural tube defects. For instance in Canada, where mandatory fortification was introduced in 1998, rates of spina bifida fell by 53 per cent.

The new UK policy will add a low level of folic acid (0.25mg per 100g flour) to non-wholemeal wheat flour.

open image in gallery A low level of folic acid will be added to flour ( Getty/iStock )

Although this new strategy is welcome, experts have already raised concerns that it will only prevent a small proportion of neural tube defects.

The government estimates that this strategy will reduce neural tube defects by around 20 per cent, preventing about 200 cases each year. But this falls short of the reduction of between 25 and 50 per cent seen in countries fully effective fortification levels.

The design of the UK scheme will also limit who benefits most. It covers only non-wholemeal wheat flour, excluding wholemeal flour, some imported products and many non-wheat flours that are important staples for some cultural and ethnic communities.

Preventing most neural tube defects requires high enough folate levels before pregnancy begins. Diet alone is unlikely to achieve this, and the proposed fortification level will provide only partial protection.

There’s also a communication risk. If people hear that flour is being fortified, they may assume supplements are no longer needed. As England’s chief medical officer, Chris Whitty, has said, fortification is a “simple and effective” way to reduce neural tube defects – but women who may become pregnant should still take a folic acid supplement before and during the first 12 weeks.

With folic acid supplement use already in decline, it’s key that women are still made aware of the benefits of using supplements before pregnancy.

Adding folic acid to flour is a long-needed step towards population-wide health. But it is not enough. The aim will be to achieve a system that combines fully effective fortification with timely education, care and support before and between pregnancies, so every woman has the best possible protection against birth defects.

Manicure lovers may be panicking that their favourite treatment is set to disappear from UK salons under the new gel nail ban.

A key ingredient used to make many brands of gel nail polish has been banned in England, Wales and Scotland.

But these new regulations do not mean Britons will be unable to get a manicure.

Here, The Independent takes a look at what will change under the new regulation.

What ingredient has been banned?

Although called the “gel nail ban” the regulation actually only bans the use of one ingredient- Trimethylbenzoyl diphenylphosphine oxide, commonly known as TPO.

open image in gallery The ingredient which allows gel polish to cure under ultraviolet (UV) light has been banned ( Getty/iStock )

This ingredient is a "photoinitiator", which allows gel polish to cure under ultraviolet (UV) light to make the varnish more durable and hold its colour for longer.

When does the gel nail ban start?

TPO has already been banned in the European Union since September 1, 2025, stopping nail technicians using this product.

But in the UK the ingredient ban only came into effect on Saturday, preventing manufacturers from selling any new products containing TPO.

open image in gallery A woman checks color samples of nail gel during the Tokyo Nail Forum ( AFP/Getty )

However, the ban is coming in gradually and the deadline for salons to stop using the product is Valentine’s Day 2027.

That means salons will be able to offer gel manicures using TPO before February next year until stocks run out - nail technicians just won’t be able to buy new stock from now on containing TPO.

The product can still be used in the US, Australia and Asia.

Why has TPO been banned?

Several animal studies have linked the chemical TPO to long-term fertility damage and reproductive issues.

open image in gallery The deadline for salons to stop using the product is Valentine’s Day 2027 ( AFP/Getty )

Caroline Rainsford, Director of Science at The Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association (CTPA), said: “The reason why TPO has been banned in cosmetic products in the EU is based on its hazardous properties, meaning how a substance might behave under a ‘worst case’ situation when our bodies are exposed to a very large amount.

“This is not how TPO is used in cosmetics. The amount of this ingredient used in nail products is over a thousand times less than the amount which could have any negative effect on fertility and these products are applied to the nail, so the potential for the ingredient to be absorbed into our bodies is even smaller.”

What will salons use instead?

TPO is only used in some gel polishes and not in traditional air-dried polishes.

There are also already TPO-free gels on the market and many salons use these products. While some alternatives may belong to the same chemical family, different compounds have different safety ratings.

Wonder Man star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II has opened up on the show’s unexpected cancellation, weeks after Marvel reversed the decision to commission a second season.

The series, which stars Abdul-Mateen as Simon Williams, a struggling actor with superpowers, drew effusive reviews when it debuted on Disney+ back in January.

It was initially announced that a second season had been greenlit; however, in July, Marvel confirmed that the show had been cancelled.

Abdul-Mateen told Vanity Fair that he had been told the decision was down to the size of its audience.

open image in gallery Yahya Abdul-Mateen II in 'Wonder Man' ( Disney Plus )

“I was told that it had something to do with the viewership numbers,” he said. “I wasn’t told what those numbers were, but ultimately, for whatever reason it was, I think they decided that it didn’t make sense for business, and that’s the decision that we live with and we keep on marching forward.”

The actor, who before Wonder Man was best known for HBO’s Watchmen and playing Morpheus in the The Matrix Resurrections, likened the cancellation to the show’s own story.

In Wonder Man, his character is an actor attempting to be cast in a remake of the film Wonder Man.

“It’s a lesson in life,” Abdul-Mateen said. “It’s so close to what real life is. You have just this guy, Simon, who finally had his dreams come true, but we saw him overcome after all of his attempts of getting close and then not closing the deal. Many people have that experience in real life. The cancellation of the show was just another one of those examples.

“I did that job for all of the right reasons, the reasons in my heart, and I had a great time doing that job,” he continued.

open image in gallery Yahya Abdul-Mateen II leads 'Wonder Man' as the titular superhero ( Marvel/Disney+ )

For his performance, Abdul-Mateen was nominated for an Emmy Award for Best Actor in a Comedy Series, with the ceremony set to take place next month.

“I’m just glad to still have an occasion to talk about the show and to represent the show.”

Speaking about a prospective second season, the actor admitted he “had my hopes and my dreams about where I wanted the character to go”.

“I was very interested in telling the story of Simon, who we watched pursue everything he’s always wanted,” he continued. And then I think, for me, the interesting question to explore is: Well, what are you going to do when you finally get it? What do you do when you finally get everything that you’ve always wanted? And for a guy like Simon to get fame and notoriety and a little bit of power, he has a big heart, but he also has an ego. He also wants to be a star.”

Wonder Man is available to stream now on Disney+.

Andy Burnham thinks Britain’s political culture is broken.

While his first few weeks in Downing Street have focussed on grassroots policy, the new prime minister has made no secret of his plan to make his premiership a “circuit breaker” for Britain, starting with the “biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen”.

The former Greater Manchester mayor wants to bring about the “end of neoliberalism” and move beyond “trickle-down economics”, rooting decision-making and power in communities, rather than centrally in London.

He said that his administration would follow a “Makerfield test”, making decisions based on whether they would improve the lives of people in constituencies like his – a brand of politics driven by lifting up those he believes have been forgotten for decades.

No 10 North, announced to much fanfare last month, is just the start of Mr Burnham’s devolution revolution. He wants far more power transferred from Westminster to local leaders and has already unveiled plans to give all mayors of England's city regions a share of income tax revenue for the first time.

open image in gallery The new prime minister's first weeks in office have focussed on bus fares, pubs and high streets ( PA Wire )

This, combined with a plan to retake public control of essential services, is the key plank in the business-friendly socialist policy agenda Mr Burnham has dubbed ‘Manchesterism’.

But to find an example of how Manchesterism could succeed, you may have to look a little further afield.

Found around 700 miles from the prime minister’s former patch, on the Nervión river which runs through Northern Spain’s Basque Country to the Bay of Biscay, Bilbao was historically a thriving port city which became a hive of heavy industry in the 20th century.

But like many port cities around the United Kingdom, it suffered the harsh impacts of deindustrialisation in the years after the Second World War, hitting a nadir in the 1980s as shipyard and factory closures caused large-scale unemployment.

“During the 80s, because we were in a quite similar situation as Liverpool and other places in England,” Ivan Jiménez, president of the Port of Bilbao, tells The Independent.

open image in gallery Ivan Jiminez, president of the Port of Bilbao ( Port of Bilbao )

“People used to say, ‘No opportunities, this is dead, the steel industry has died.’

“Here, in the 80s, I remember that we here had a 25 per cent unemployment rate. It was devastated.”

But the Bilbao of 2026 has come a long way since the 1980s, and its recovery will be of particular interest to the UK’s new prime minister.

Once home to the city’s maritime might, the banks of the river are now most notable for the Guggenheim museum, built in 1997 to become the ship-shaped symbol of its revival.

Between its opening and 2015, GDP in the city more than doubled as it pivoted from a declining steel and shipbuilding economy to become a hub of clean energy, advanced manufacturing and biotechnology, with tourism and culture becoming key economies.

From 2000 to 2018, the city had the highest level of economic growth in Spain and, according to Mr Jiménez, that owes a lot to its devolved powers, similar to those Mr Burnham wishes to introduce in the UK.

Bilbao‘s province Biscay is one of three which make up the autonomous community of the Basque Country, a region marked by a prominent separatist movement, part of which desires complete independence from Spain.

But the Basque Country’s self-governance means it has sweeping powers over tax, education, health, economic strategy and welfare.

As such, residents do not pay state income tax.

Instead of being funded by the Spanish central government in Madrid, Bilbao collects 100 per cent of its own income tax through its three provinces and keeps the majority, sending a fixed annual quota to the capital to pay for national services, such as the military.

open image in gallery Bilbao has seen a significant transformation in recent years ( cimata - stock.adobe.com )

Mr Burnham hopes that a similarly less centralised approach would revive the fortunes of Britain’s post-industrial regions. Ensuring that money and power are not concentrated in London is central to his agenda.

And, like in Bilbao, taxation could be key to that.

Last month, the prime minister announced that mayors in England will get to keep a share of taxes collected in their regions to “bring power home” to communities.

The regional leaders will receive a share of income tax revenues for the first time under the plans, which the government has described as the “biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”, and would bolster their funding - on top of settlements currently allocated by central government.

Such autonomy has helped Bilbao thrive, according to Mr Jiménez it proves that “you can manage without the dependency from the central state”.

“At the end, about 90 per cent of the taxes that are collected in the Basque Country stay in the Basque Country.

“With this autonomy, and in collaboration also with different other institutions - also from the state, also from Europe - they transformed a city that was based on heavy industry to advanced services and new industries.”

Mr Jiménez believes that consistent public investment through locally-collected income taxes has allowed the region to develop in a way that suits itself, rather than having a path chosen for it by central government.

But this has been boosted, he says, by tailored private investment and collaboration with the public sector, such as the public-private partnership Bilbao Ría 2000, tasked with regenerating post-industrial sites.

open image in gallery The distinctive Guggenheim museum helped transform Bilbao's fortunes ( Fernando - stock.adobe.com )

“Collaboration is quite easy here”, Mr Jiménez says. To have a meeting here with any kind of politician for an entrepreneur, it's quite easy.

“They used to tell us, for example, you go to Madrid or other places to have a meeting with the regional ministry, it's quite difficult.

“In our case, the doors are always open because we are looking all the time for investment, research, development.”

It is, in many ways, redolent of what the MP for Makerfield wishes to achieve with his flagship policy of Number 10 North. Rather than everything being delivered through a nation’s capital, he hopes his new Manchester outpost will mean meetings for investment do not have to take place centrally.

Where Mr Burnham may struggle however, is installing such a devolved economic system from scratch, Mr Jiménez says.

It is not a case of one size fits all, he believes, and such plans have to be bespoke in each region.

Though the English mayors have powers over matters such as transport and in their combined authorities, giving them control of taxes represents a radical change to the system.

open image in gallery Number 10 North is an early flagship policy of Andy Burnham's ( PA Media )

And for Mr Jiménez, the reason it works in the Basque Country is its historic autonomy.

“If you ask me, nowadays, could it be possible to create this from zero in the Spanish state? I would find it very, very difficult”, he explains.

“If you want to translate this to any other place, and if you don't have a culture - a culture in our case coming from history - it could be a very difficult talk or discussion.

“That's very clear, and would probably be much easier to implement this in a place where this identity plays a main role.”

Strong identity and pride – whether it is national in the case of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland or regional in places like the Liverpool City Region (where a ‘Scouse not English’ attitude exists) – and ensuring people believe that their part of the UK can thrive is key to making it work.

Mr Jiménez added: “You say: ‘I may feel English or not English but I'm very linked to my region, and even if I feel English 100 per cent, I want to promote, I want to stay here, I want my children and grandchildren to grow up here with a lot of opportunities.’”

Retaining talent in the Basque Country is the job of Amaia Jugo, managing director of Bizkaia Talent.

open image in gallery Amaia Jugo, managing director of Bizkaia Talent ( Supplied )

When opening No 10 North, the prime minister recalled his own experience of moving to London as a graduate in the early 1990s to find work, as he promised to make that a thing of the past.

To and allow people to build their lives in their home towns and cities, he has also pledged a project of reindustrialization, not dissimilar to that in the Basque Country, bringing a green energy revolution to areas which lost their core industries in the 20th century.

About how the Basque Country has done so and prevents a brain drain, Ms Jugo said: “We explain that we have very good opportunities in strategic industries. We have different clusters, like automation, where you can have very good opportunities.

“When young people finish university, they are usually looking at London or Madrid. It is very important to be connected with them to show that they will have good opportunities here and can do a very good job in companies that have a good impact in our ecosystem.

“We have to change. We know that some industries are going to disappear or become smaller. So we have to understand that we need different industries.”

News.title: Wildfires across Europe detonate forgotten World War bombs
News.content:

Scorched landscapes across Europe have exposed a potentially lethal threat lurking underground.

Rusted bombs and mines from the First and Second World Wars are now endangering emergency crews responding to the wildfires across the continent.

High heat has caused several weapons to explode in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands. In the Dutch province of Limburg, a bomb-disposal team was called out to inspect woodland near the site of heavy 1944 combat threatened by flames.

Exacerbated by climate change, the blazes and detonations show that Europe’s "climatic luck" is ending, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London’s School of Oriental and African Studies. Consistent temperatures and predictable rain previously kept hidden weapons dormant.

"Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable," Ms Njeri said. Blazes can ignite vintage munitions and clear away the dense brush concealing them.

Heavy rainfall in January spurred vegetation growth that turned to kindling when summer heat arrived. Coupled with drought, low humidity and stiff winds, the temperatures created optimal conditions for fire, according to a World Weather Attribution study published in July.

open image in gallery Members of a bomb disposal unit, Dieter Schwaetzler, left, and Rene Bennert sit next to an 1.8-tonne Second World War bomb after defusing it in Frankfurt, Germany, in 2017 ( AP )

As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns of the World Wars fell silent.

In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be Second World War-era ammunition.

In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Governor Hervé Jamar said that “a few sporadic detonations" were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in fire areas. He said that no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb.

During the Second World War, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province's dense peat-bog forest, which is known as the High Fens.

In the first four years after Germany’s surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium's border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war.

open image in gallery Bernard Collard runs a metal detector over a field in the Elsenborn area of Krinkelt, Belgium ( AP )

“When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are,” he said.

The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smouldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops in the famed Battle of the Bulge.

The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and saw about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops killed.

‘It’s part of our history’

Mr Collard is authorised to scan the former battlefields, which are now forests, pastures and farmland, with a metal detector. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton.

“You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn’t take it lightly,” he said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes covered old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire.

Mr Collard frequently works with the Belgian de-mining squad. “It’s part of our history. We live with it,” he said.

Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany.

open image in gallery Smoke rises from a field scorched by a wildfire near Waimes, Belgium ( AP )

The Belgian Ministry of Defence said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a “hot spot” compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres, which is infamous for harrowing trench warfare in the Second World War, call the annual tilling of the soil “the iron harvest” because it turns up so many war remnants.

Every year across the nation, Belgium’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars.

Drought also poses a threat

Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons.

In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest's Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from the Second World War emerged at its base in receding water.

As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a Second World War-era bomb.

Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Ms Njeri, wrote an article on Europe’s wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said “the legacy of war keeps creeping up” because of climate change.

“It's reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven't had to deal with in a while in certain places."

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Liverpool make Real Madrid enquiry after Minteh bid rejected and Man Utd seal Baleba deal after Arsenal confirm Konsa

Close With the new Premier League season on the very immediate horizon, Adam Clery explores Arsenal's chances of retaining their title for the first time since the 1930s

Arsenal are exploring a move for Juventus forward Kenan Yildiz as Mikel Arteta seeks to complete his transfer plans for an assault on both the Champions League and Premier League for the new season. The Gunners are agreed to sign Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa, but the left side of attack has long been identified as a priority position and the 21-year-old Turkey international is high up on their list of targets.

Liverpool have had a £50m offer for Yankuba Minteh rebuffed by Brighton, as they step up their search for a successor to Mohamed Salah, and have agreed a deal with Inter Milan to sell Curtis Jones. Liverpool are also interested in Bradley Barcola, but there has been a substantial difference in their valuation of the France international and Paris Saint-Germain’s, with the Champions League winners looking for £145m.

Manchester United are ready to splash more than £60m on Brighton’s Carlos Baleba, ending a pursuit that begun last summer and bringing in further reinforcements to their midfield, while Tottenham have agreed a deal to sign Manchester City winger Savinho for an initial £75m.
