World.title: Azerbaijan’s ambassador to Costa Rica presents credentials to President (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Seymur Fataliyev, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Azerbaijan to Costa Rica, presented his credentials to Laura Fernández, President of the Republic of Costa Rica.

This was reported by the Azerbaijani Embassy in Costa Rica.

In addition, it was reported that the ambassador conveyed sincere greetings and best wishes from the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, to the President of Costa Rica. President Laura Fernández expressed her gratitude and asked that her sincere greetings be conveyed to the President of Azerbaijan.

During the meeting, the ambassador briefed President Laura Fernández on Azerbaijan’s growing role against the backdrop of recent geopolitical developments in the region and emerging new realities, as well as on the country’s economic potential and favorable investment climate. In addition, he highlighted important achievements in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

President Laura Fernández congratulated Azerbaijan on the progress made in the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia. She expressed her readiness to continue joint efforts aimed at further developing friendly relations and cooperation between Costa Rica and Azerbaijan during her presidential term. The President of Costa Rica wished the Azerbaijani ambassador success in his diplomatic work.

The ambassador also presented President Laura Fernández with a book published by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation titled “Azerbaijan: Captivated by the Charms of Nature.”

World.title: Uzbekistan’s Fergana region explores new industrial projects with Germany
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Uzbekistan’s Fergana region is exploring new opportunities for industrial cooperation with Germany, including the development of manufacturing, construction, healthcare, pharmaceuticals and information technology projects.

This was reflected in the statement by the Fergana Regional Administration, following a meeting between Governor Khayrullo Bozorov, Bakhrom Tulaganov, rector of the Tashkent University of Architecture and Civil Engineering, and Abduvakhob Dadamakhammmedov, head of Germany’s ABM Anlagenbau & Maschinentechnik GmbH in Central Asia.

According to the Regional Administration, the meeting focused on expanding interregional cooperation, establishing new partnerships and developing joint initiatives between Fergana and German businesses.

''The parties emphasized that effective cooperation requires identifying specific needs and opportunities, developing proposals that meet modern requirements, and implementing them through clearly defined plans,'' the Regional Administration says, citing the meeting.

Particular attention was given to the experience of ABM Anlagenbau & Maschinentechnik GmbH in supplying industrial enterprises with modern equipment, introducing technological solutions and improving production processes.

Based on the company’s expertise, the sides discussed potential areas for expanded cooperation with German partners, including industrial cooperation in Fergana, mechanical engineering, construction, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, information technology, livestock production and manufacturing.

The meeting also highlighted the importance of transforming potential areas of cooperation into concrete investment and industrial projects.

''Effective cooperation should be based on a thorough assessment of specific needs and opportunities, followed by the development and implementation of practical projects,'' the participants noted.

Following the meeting, the sides agreed to identify priority areas for cooperation and continue negotiations aimed at developing them into concrete projects.

World.title: Hazar Logistik sees rail links via Akina, Turghundi as key Afghan routes (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. Turkmenistan's Hazar Logistics sees rail routes through Akina and Turghundi as the most promising links for expanding transport cooperation with Afghanistan.

The company made the assessment in an exclusive response to Trend's questions about the outcomes of its August 6 meeting with a Herat delegation and prospects for developing bilateral logistics routes.

"Hazar Logistik considers railway routes passing through the Akina and Turghundi border crossings, which connect Afghanistan with Turkmenistan's transport infrastructure, to be the most promising," the company said.

According to Hazar Logistik, these routes could connect Afghanistan with Turkmenistan's railway network, the International Seaport of Turkmenbashi and international transport corridors.

"Of particular importance are routes integrated with Turkmenistan's railway network, the International Seaport of Turkmenbashi and international transport corridors, creating additional opportunities for cargo delivery to the Caspian region, the Caucasus, Europe and other destinations," the company noted.

The company said potential cargo flows could include several categories of goods as trade ties between the two countries develop.

"With further development of trade and economic cooperation, potential cargo flows could include construction materials, oil and gas and industrial equipment, agricultural and food products, mineral fertilizers, petroleum products, containerized cargo and other goods," Hazar Logistik said.

Hazar Logistik also considers the Afghan direction promising for the further development of international logistics, although it did not provide specific cargo growth forecasts.

"Hazar Logistik considers the Afghan direction one of the promising areas for further development of international logistics," the company added.

According to the company, future cargo growth will depend on the development of foreign trade ties, joint infrastructure projects, market demand and the formation of sustainable logistics chains.

The company also highlighted Turkmenistan's potential as a transit link connecting Afghanistan and Central Asia with the Caspian region and international markets.

"Thanks to its favorable geographical location and consistent state policy aimed at developing international transport corridors, Turkmenistan has significant potential as an important transit link between Central Asia, Afghanistan, the Caspian region and international markets," the company said.

According to Hazar Logistik, the August 6 meeting with the Herat delegation resulted in an agreement to continue professional dialogue, exchange necessary information and assess potential areas of cooperation.

The company said the next stage would involve further consultations and work on organizational and technical aspects of possible joint projects, including logistics solutions, transport routes and cooperation mechanisms in accordance with international conventions and Turkmenistan's legislation.

Hazar Logistik is a Turkmen transport and logistics company providing container, rail, road, sea, air and multimodal transportation services. The company handles import, export and transit operations and provides cargo transportation services across Turkmenistan, the CIS and international destinations. Its services are covered by licenses for maritime transportation, transport and forwarding activities and road freight services, while its management system is certified under the ISO 9001:2015 international standard.

The company has branches and offices in Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, China, Türkiye, Georgia and the UAE, including offices in Poti and Istanbul. Its services include rail freight, customs clearance, container transportation, maritime shipping and multimodal logistics. Hazar Logistik is also included in the official register of customs brokers maintained by the Customs Service of Turkmenistan under registration code GD-0066.

World.title: Sydney childcare centre on brink of closure offered 12-months rent free
World.content:
A not-for-profit early learning centre on the brink of closure has been handed a lifeline, with more than 60 families rallying in Sydney's eastern suburbs to keep the doors open.

The threatened closure of Goodstart East Sydney in Darlinghurst triggered a petition this week after the centre informed families that the site was shuttering from November 26.

Goodstart had been leasing the site from the City of Sydney but said the design and location of the building meant the centre was making a significant loss, despite high occupancy.

Parents rally to show their support for the centre. (ABC News: Alexander Lewis)

In response Lord Mayor Clover Moore offered the early learning centre 12 months free rent while its future is resolved.

"I hope this gives comfort and certainty to parents that we are committed to ensuring stability and the learning community they have built in Darlo [Darlinghurst]," Cr Moore wrote in a Facebook post.

It is unclear if the provider, which leases three other sites from the City of Sydney, has accepted the rent waiver.

The ABC has reached out for comment.

'There aren't many options in the area'

On Saturday, Tim Martin was among dozens of families at Potts Point who rallied in support of the centre.

"Losing the centre would be so devastating," the father-of-two said.

"What we really feel for is the staff of the centre too, they probably won't have jobs."

Mr Martin says losing the centre would be "devastating". (ABC News)

Mr Martin said he and his wife had already canvassed close to six centres nearby.

"They're all full, some have a day here or there, but it's just not doable."

Three centres in the local area have recently closed. Another not-for-profit in Paddington could also be lost as the site is earmarked to be sold.

Fiona Thatcher said her 11-month-old daughter Mave had been on the centre's waiting list since she was 12-weeks-old.

"I don't think many of us have much of a plan B because there aren't many options in the area at all," she said.

"It would certainly involve enrolling in multiple centres, driving quite a distance … it would also mean losing the educators, which was the primary motivators for getting together like this."

Ms Thatcher says there are not many childcare options in the area. (ABC News: Alexander Lewis)

Ms Thatcher said she did not think the area could accommodate the 60 families enrolled at the childcare centre and the more than 100 on its waiting list.

Labor Councillor Zann Maxwell said the demand was there, but the provider had given "mixed messages" about the site's closure.

"The last thing we want to see is the loss of a childcare centre in the inner-city," he said.

"We want to be making sure that this is the kind of place where all sorts of people can live, including young families, and we're not serious about it if we let places like this close."

World.title: Quick hits: Stunning Shoriful rivals Starc's staggering spell, Hazlewood fumes
World.content:
Two lethal left arm quicks combine for 12 wickets, Australia comes close to snaring the rarest of dismissals, and a Harrup Park specialist fails on his return to the team.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Sensational Starc's first-ball strike

Mitchell Starc claimed a first ball wicket in both of this first two overs. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

We've seen this play before: Four times, in fact.

Mitch Starc steaming in, an opening batter studiously preparing for a lengthy stay at the crease, only to succumb to the very first challenge.

Shadman Islam was the unfortunate batter on this occasion, looking to clip Starc into the leg side but misjudging the pace and sending a leading edge to Cameron Green at gully.

He is, incredibly, the fourth batter to fall to Starc with the very first ball of a Test match.

Sri Lankan opener Dimuth Karunaratne was his first such victim back in 2016.

England's Rory Burns was famously bowled around his legs at the Gabba in the 2021/22 Ashes series.

And then, in 2024 at Adelaide Oval, Yashavi Jaiswal was trapped LBW with a pink ball.

Oh, and he wasn't done there, either.

2. Starc's five-fa comes in just 22 balls

Mitchell Starc tore through the top order. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Mitch Starc would not be contained or limited with just one wicket in his first spell.

Incredibly, he took five, tearing through the Bangladesh top order like a cyclone of ill-intent.

Shadman Islam's wicket was the only one to fall in the first over.

But in his second, he took two in the first two balls, accounting for Tanzid and Shanto in consecutive balls.

Mominul survived the first ball of the third over, but shouldn't have let down his guard as he fell later in the very same over to make it 4 in 3 for the big left-hander.

And then, in his fourth over, he made it five, Litton Das falling LBW for yet another duck, his five wickets coming in just 22 balls.

It should have been just 21 balls, had Beau Webster not shelled the sort of ball that you'd toss up to a toddler in the backyard.

It didn't matter though, Starc could not be contained, ending his six-over spell with figures of 5-5 and four maidens, leaving Bangladesh 5-15.

It was the sixth fastest five-wicket haul in Test history, but remarkably, it wasn't Starc's fastest in the format — that came in just 15 balls against the West Indies last year.

3. Obstructing the field?

Hazlewood was unimpressed with Taskin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Fans of obscure dismissals were almost gifted a rare instance of a player obstructing the field in the later stages of Bangladesh's batting innings.

Hazlewood came in and Taskin swiped across the line, sending the ball straight up in the air.

Hazlewood raced towards the ball, as Taskin took off for a run, before he then realised Hazlewood was baring down on him.

Taskin attempted to cover up, Hazlewood barged into him and the ball fell safe.

The crowd in Mackay felt aggrieved and there was more than a small suggestion of obstructing the field.

Hazlewood's eyes were in danger of having to be registered as dangerous weapons such was the ferocity of the daggers he was giving the unfortunate batter, as Pat Cummins engaged in a discussion with umpire Nitin Menon.

There was no appeal though that we could see, and Taskin was reprieved.

Only one player has ever been given out obstructing the field in Test cricket, Len Hutton for England against South Africa at The Oval in 1951.

Incredibly, later in the over, it appeared there was an (inadvertent) case of a double hit too as an attempted pull shot went awry.

4. Renshaw out cheaply on Test return

Renshaw was dimissed cheaply on his return to the Test arena. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

If Matt Renshaw could have chosen any ground in the world to make his Test return, it may well have been Harrup Park.

The Queenslander is the leading First Class run scorer at the venue, and is the only man to have scored two Sheffield Shield centuries in Mackay.

He's also coming off an impressive domestic summer, during which he scored three red-ball centuries at an average flirting with 50.

And it was under porcelain blue skies and in what looked to be perfect batting conditions that he made his way back to the Test-match crease, with the pitch having flattened out since Starc's new-ball demolition job.

The southpaw made an assured start to his innings, working a few attractive runs through the off-side, but it wasn't long before he was back in the sheds, having edged one into the slips.

Renshaw was out for 8 and Bangladesh, in desperate need of an early wicket after being bundled out for just 64, had their breakthrough.

5. Shoriful's dream day

The towering Shoriful made an instant impact at the bowling crease. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Forced to sit out the first Test with a side strain, exciting fast bowler Shoriful Islam wasted no time in making an impact in Mackay.

The 25-year-old left-armer is just that little bit quicker than his more workmanlike pace-bowling colleagues, and at over 190 centimetres tall, provides a different challenge in terms of release point.

Coming into the attack at first change, Shoriful took just two deliveries to claim his first Test wicket in Australia.

Pitching on a good length and seaming into Travis Head, the Australian opener was caught trying to play a shot that was never there, and was out chopping on for the third innings in a row.

Three balls later, and Shoriful had his second.

This time, he was aided by thigh pad rather than willow, with the ball rolling onto the stumps after thudding into Marnus Labuschagne.

Labuschagne was in disbelief, Shoriful was in dreamland, and Bangladesh was making a fist of things in Mackay.

And the towering left-armer wasn't done there.

First, he produced a beauty to dismiss Smith, who was well set on 42, LBW midway through the evening session.

Then, he tore through the Australian lower order, conjuring three more moments of magic to dismiss Beau Webster and Cummins for ducks, and Starc for 1.

World.title: Pendlebury could miss rest of season with his playing future undecided
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury's glittering Collingwood career could be over after the AFL/VFL games record holder suffered a hamstring injury.

The 38-year-old will miss up to three weeks, ruling him out of at least next week's historic wildcard match.

In an added blow for the Magpies, tough defender Brayden Maynard suffered a knee injury at training and is in doubt to return this season, no matter how far Collingwood progress in finals.

"These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden," Collingwood football boss Charlie Gardiner said.

"These are unfortunate setbacks especially at this time of year, but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible."

Pendlebury was ruled out in the second quarter of Friday night's 63-point thrashing by Brisbane at the MCG with what Collingwood described as a "knee bursa".

But scans on Saturday revealed a hamstring strain that will sideline him for two or three weeks.

It comes at a critical time for the 21-season veteran, who is waiting until the end of the year to decide if he plays on in 2027.

McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

If he does not retire, Pendlebury has also received an offer from Gold Coast to be effectively an on-field playing coach next year.

Collingwood are carefully balancing how they deal with an iconic player contemplating his football mortality.

Pendlebury was also substituted four-and-a-half minutes into last year's preliminary-final loss to Brisbane with calf tightness.

Collingwood would likely err on the side of caution, desperate to avoid a repeat, even if the Magpies are still in premiership contention when he is available.

The Magpies would have to play five straight weeks of knockout finals to claim the most unlikely of premierships.

"That'll all be weighed up," coach Craig McRae said.

"He (Maynard) might be right to go, but then do we want to take that risk?"

The Magpies were conservative with Isaac Quaynor, Patrick Lipinski and Maynard on Friday night.

All three were expected to return next week, but Maynard is now no chance.

"Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade-one MCL strain," Gardiner said.

"This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury."

Collingwood also managed the game time of Nick Daicos and Darcy Cameron against the Lions in anticipation of the wildcard game, which McRae insisted felt like a final.

AAP

World.title: US, Canada fail to reach tariff deal, deepen trade war
World.content:
The United States has imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $US20 billion ($27.9 billion) worth of Canadian products and Canada says it will retaliate.

Last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain in already tense relations between the historical allies.

US President Donald Trump's import taxes will hit about 5 per cent of what Canada ships to the United States every year, including products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.

US to impose 50pc tariffs on most Canadian goods The White House says the tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, meaning there is time for negotiations.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said his nation would match the US tariffs dollar for dollar, escalating the trade conflict and calling into question the future of a North American trade pact between the United States, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.

Canada sought concessions on tariffs on steel, aluminium, autos and lumber that the United States was unwilling to provide.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement, early Saturday local time: "Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.

"Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Canada have up-ended the careful balance reached in the past days," the statement said.

Mr Carney responded: "Last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."

He said his government would announce additional support for Canadian workers and businesses in the coming days.

Mr Greer said the US offer was "forward-looking" and included "a historic economic and national security partnership".

No further talks have been planned.

The breakdown in negotiations marked a sharp reversal from two days earlier, when officials from the two countries sounded as if they were headed toward a compromise.

Typically cooperative alliance goes sour

The political impact will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $US880 billion worth of goods and services last year.

The tariffs were initially supposed to kick in at 12:01am on Wednesday.

Donald Trump said on Friday that he expected the US to strike a trade deal with Canada. (AP: Manuel Balce Ceneta)

Mr Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue, but the two countries still could not reach an agreement in time.

The two nations have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots like Canadian softwood lumber imports and US access to Canada's protected dairy market.

Somehow, they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners.

Mr Trump's approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries.

He has hit Canadian goods with tariffs, in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States, and has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America's 51st state.

Canadians and Americans are frustrated

The Canadian public is fed up.

A petition to expel the US ambassador, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 248,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of having "normalised'' Mr Trump's talk of annexing Canada, among other things.

The two countries had good reasons to find a compromise.

Donald Trump's import taxes will apply to about 5 per cent of what Canada ships to the US every year. (AP: Mark Schiefelbein)

Nearly 72 per cent of Canada's goods exports last year went to the United States.

And the Trump administration might be wary of imposing a hefty new tariff, paid by US importers who try to pass on the cost to consumers via higher prices, ahead of November’s midterm elections.

American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.

"Canada likely wanted further sector-specific relief than the US was willing to offer, or Canada's concessions did not go far enough,'' said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former US trade official.

Smoke risks looms for World Cup Fears that wildfire smoke could disrupt the World Cup final remain, as US president Donald Trump threatens Canada with tariffs.

"Either way, I think both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to still find an off-ramp. But if Canada has agreed to also impose tariffs, the off-ramp may be even harder to find."

Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, called the tariffs "a body blow to North American competitiveness", warning they would raise costs for Americans while threatening Canadian customers, investment and small businesses.

The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew a trade agreement that Mr Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph.

The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico over revamping the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). But talks with Canada have not begun, and the escalating trade conflict casts doubt on whether they will.

"Canada told the Americans in advance that if these tariffs landed, it would stop negotiating and retaliate,'' said Barry Appleton, senior fellow at the Center for International Law at New York Law School.

"The American trade representative said publicly he would not tolerate retaliation. Both sides have now committed themselves in public, which is how escalation stops being a choice.''

AP

World.title: Adelaide lacrosse community turns out to support girl, 5, with leukaemia
World.content:
Within days of five-year-old Margot Whinnen being diagnosed and treated for acute myeloid leukaemia, a tight-knit sports community has rallied in support.

Margot was diagnosed with the blood cancer last Saturday after she had described painful symptoms, prompting her parents Jesse and Nicole to take her for tests.

"She was really bad, complaining of a stomach ache, she couldn't move, so we decided to take her in," said Mr Whinnen.

"The blood test came back with some surprising results so she got transferred to the Women's and Children's and then we found out it was acute myeloid leukaemia."

Margot immediately began chemotherapy at the Women's and Children's Hospital, where she remains.

Mr Whinnen said Margot will undertake four rounds of treatment and will likely remain in hospital for months.

" We've just got to deal with it and hopefully she pulls through with flying colours. "

Lacrosse community comes together

In support of the Whinnen family, the South Australian lacrosse community held a fundraising fete dubbed 'Stick It 2 Leukaemia' in Brighton on Saturday, with hundreds in attendance.

A GoFundMe page established to support the family has raised more than $63,000.

"[It's] pretty overwhelming, very emotional but amazing that the whole community has gotten behind Margot and behind our family. We really appreciate it from everyone," said Mr Whinnen.

Traci Mathwin, a director of Lacrosse South Australia, said support for the Whinnen family had come in from across the globe.

"I drove up here this morning and you expect people to be a part of it, but I didn't expect people to be this involved," Ms Mathwin said.

"The kids, probably some of them don't understand, but the fact that they get to support Margot and Jesse and Nicole and [their] boys, Logan and Miles, is fabulous, it means a lot.

"Our community is a really tight community, so when things like this happen, even worldwide, World Lacrosse is on board."

World.title: For years, one man spearheaded a Nigerian government agency that didn't exist
World.content:
On paper, the Nigerian Presidential Foreign Intervention Promotion Council (PFIPC) looked every bit like an official government agency.

It had funding, an office inside the Federal Secretariat in Abuja, which houses many government ministries, and a website bearing the government's stamp of authenticity. Few reasons existed to question its legitimacy.

Until it emerged that the agency did not officially exist.

The revelation has triggered wider scrutiny of government institutions, with a second organisation, the National Brands Development and Made in Nigeria Special Project Office (NBDMNSPO), now also under investigation.

Here is how both agencies managed to operate under the radar.

A budget of $1 million

For years, Prince Adeniyi Adeyemi Matthew walked Nigeria's government halls as the "Director-General" of the PFIPC.

The role of the agency was purportedly to attract foreign investment, aid and partnerships into Africa's most populous country.

It had what looked like a legitimate website, maintained a social media presence, and even won approval to hire more than 300 staff.

The Instagram account of the fictitious PFIPC is still active. (Instagram:_pfipc)

Adeyemi even met with government officials, including cabinet ministers, financial regulators, the head of Nigeria's anti-corruption agency and foreign diplomats.

So, after almost two years, what triggered the alarm bells?

Well, in 2025, officials from the Nigerian Investment Promotion Council wrote to the presidency to complain about Adeyemi's activities, noting that his agency appeared to function at "cross-purposes" with it.

Then a few months later, Femi Gbajabiamila, the president's chief of staff, wrote to police alleging that his signature, along with official seals and reference numbers, had been forged by Adeyemi.

"The fake documents, bearing falsified signatures, reference/folio numbers, and seals, have been used to claim leadership appointments to non-existent entities, with particular reference to the PFIPC," Gbajabiamila wrote.

Local reports said Adeyemi claimed he was given the PFIPC director-general appointment letter by Gbajabiamila, who has denied knowing him.

"Politicians and members of the public who are weaponising Adeyemi's claim against the chief of staff should refrain from swallowing his narrative hook, line and sinker," the presidency said in a statement defending Gbajabiamila.

In a July 1, 2026 statement, the Nigerian presidency also claimed Adeyemi misled the country's accountant-general's office into opening 34 bank accounts for the PFIPC, including with the Central Bank of Nigeria.

The fake agencies flew under Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's nose. (Reuters: Kin Cheung)

When the 2026 national budget was signed into law, the PFIPC was included with an allocation of 1.3 billion naira ($1.3 million).

However, according to the police and the accountant-general's office, no government money was transferred into any of the bank accounts.

Following the revelation, Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu directed the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) to investigate and submit a comprehensive report.

The report, published on August 8, found Adeyemi was never appointed by "any authority of government" and that he should be prosecuted.

It stressed that the investigation was still ongoing, particularly to identify other persons who may have participated in or facilitated the alleged scheme.

What about the other fake agency?

There is little information on the NBDMNSPO.

That is because its discovery as a fake agency was only recently announced by the ICPC.

However, the ICPC did reveal the NBDMNSPO was spearheaded by George Buchi Nwabueze, who allegedly operated with the assistance of suspected collaborators within the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (OSGF).

A photo that purports to be George Buchi Nwabueze. (Instagram: pmainpro)

It said the investigation found that Nwabueze used four variations of his name while running the illegal operation.

Musa Adamu Aliyu, the head of the ICPC, did not say whether Nwabueze had profited from the scheme before it was uncovered.

On the NBDMNSPO website's "vision and mission page", it says the agency's purpose is "Transforming The National From A Resource Dependent Nation Into A Vibrant Hub of Production Oriented Manufacturing Country".

What were they charged with?

Adeyemi was charged with eight offences, including forgery and impersonation.

After failing to appear at a hearing to face the charges, the Federal High Court issued a warrant for Adeyemi.

After weeks in hiding fearing his safety, he was arrested in Osun State in south-western Nigeria.

Adeyemi has maintained his innocence in interviews with local media.

Two of his accomplices have also been charged.

Meanwhile, authorities have issued an arrest warrant for Nwabueze while his collaborators MS Danjuma, Engr Nandungu Gagare and Richard Pheelangwa were suspended from the OSGF.

World.title: Live: Big men dominating as Warriors lead Rabbitohs
World.content:
Newcastle have thrown their home-final hopes into jeopardy after capitulating to Manly in a shock 44-24 humbling on Old Boys' Day.

On a chaotic Saturday in Newcastle, the Knights blew an 18-6 lead early to leave themselves potentially needing to beat the Warriors next week to stay sixth.

They also face the prospect of starting the finals without Dom Young, who was sin-binned for a hip-drop tackle that left Sea Eagles star Tolu Koula with a syndesmosis injury.

The result also kept Manly's faint finals hopes alive, as Kieran Foran's men snapped a six-game losing streak and showed off the attacking strike that had them firing mid-season.

Albeit remote, the Sea Eagles need to beat St George Illawarra and the Warriors, while also relying on South Sydney or North Queensland going winless for the rest of the year.

Manly will be left wondering where this kind of attacking strike has been for the past two months, after sliding from third to only a mathematical chance of playing finals.

Centre Josh Feledy scored a hat-trick while filling in for Kolu at centre, while Clayton Faulalo impressed in his first game in the No.6 jersey.

Tom Trbojevic also looked dangerous on return, despite being felled a number of times during the match and at one stage being victim to a Tyson Frizzel hip-drop tackle.

The Sea Eagles went after Newcastle's right edge at will, opening the scoring in the third minute when Lehi Hopoate set Faulalo free.

Manly were then vulnerable themselves down that side while Faulalo was off for a head injury assessment, with Kalyn Ponga, Fletcher Sharpe and Dom Young wreaking havoc as the Knights went 16-6 up.

But the game swung dramatically when Newcastle took a penalty goal to lead 18-6 and Jermaine McEwan coughed up possession on the next set.

From there, Tom Trbojevic sent Caleb Navale over for one try on his return from an ACL rupture, and Feledy scored twice in the space of four minutes with Young in the bin to make it 24-18.

The Sea Eagles ran away with the game in the second half, again attacking the Knights edges.

Newcastle are assured of a top-eight spot, but this was a sobering reminder of the challenge that remains after rising up from last year's wooden spoon.

Dane Gagai could return from a hamstring injury in time for the finals, but any ban for Young will cause more issues on their right side.

AAP

World.title: Delhi's electric tuktuk boom gets a hacking shock
World.content:
Few sights and sounds are as familiar in Delhi as colourful auto rickshaws and the rhythmic beat of their engines.

The same could be said of the Indian capital's notorious air pollution, fed in part by the three-wheelers' belching exhausts.

Indrajeet Sachdeva has been driving one for decades, earning a few hundred rupees a day.

Now, he says his career is at risk after Delhi's government announced a ban on new non-electric rickshaws from January 2027.

From April 2028, the ban will extend to new motorcycles and scooters as well, slowly replacing more than 6 million small vehicles registered in the city in a bid to clean its persistent smog.

"This policy is like bringing a mongoose to kill a snake. What will we do if the mongoose kills us?" Mr Sachdeva said.

More than 95,000 auto rickshaws are registered in the Delhi National Capital Territory. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Tuktuk no more

Since the 50s, rickshaws with two-stroke engines have become notorious for their iconic tuktuk sound and smoky exhausts, contributing to harmful smog in Delhi and other large Asian cities.

India's Supreme Court mandated Delhi's rickshaws switch to compressed natural gas (CNG) in 2001 to help clean the city's air, but the problem hasn't gone away.

In 2025, air quality tracking service IQAir ranked Delhi's urban area as the most polluted on Earth.

Delhi's toxic smog compared to smoking 50 cigarettes a day Delhi's notorious air pollution kills thousands. Can it be fixed?

"Estimates vary between one-third to 50 per cent [of Delhi's pollution] coming from transport," International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) India director Amit Bhatt said.

"We've found that CNG vehicles are not so clean when it comes to nitrogen oxide emissions, and nitrogen oxides lead to secondary particulate matter [in the air]."

Despite the persistent pollution, many rickshaw drivers still consider CNG a clean alternative to petrol and fear losing their income to another change.

"I have been driving an auto since 2002 and [an electric rickshaw] costs 250,000 to 300,000 rupees ($3,700-$4,400)," rickshaw driver Suraj Kumar Gupta said.

" If I buy in this age, I would be tired paying interest on the loan. Either the auto will get old or I will. "

Mr Sachdeva, who leads a welfare group for rickshaw drivers in the city, said they were planning a legal challenge before the restrictions in January.

Electric rickshaw revolution

Sunitha Anup is a researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation in India. (ABC News: Som Patidar)

Regardless of the challenge, they may soon be outnumbered by others who have already switched.

ICCT researcher Sunitha Anup said their analysis indicated around half of India's rickshaws were already electric, a far higher percentage than any other class of vehicle.

"For four-wheelers, it's around 4 per cent," she said.

Other South and South-East Asian countries have also embraced electric scooters, motorcycles and rickshaws far more than electric cars.

India's micro-EV boom has been partly supported by imported components that can be easily adapted for use by local manufacturers.

However, just days after Delhi's cabinet signed its new EV policy into law, the drivers of those affordable electric rickshaws were given a rude shock.

Battery hacking

In July, videos began to spread online showing electric rickshaws stopping dead on Delhi's streets.

The hack was simple and spread quickly: scammers would download a free battery management app, scan for passing vehicles with unsecured Bluetooth connections, then use the app to disable the battery remotely.

Loading Instagram content

Some would use this opportunity to extort money from the driver.

The Indian government responded quickly, ordering Google and Apple to remove some Chinese battery management apps from app stores.

Experts have warned that many of Delhi's electric rickshaws are still vulnerable.

"These [banned] apps are not the only apps; anybody can write such an app and share it," International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad director Sandeep Kumar Shukla said.

"We have these battery packs being imported and being fitted into vehicles without any cybersecurity compliance check.

" In fact, there is no guideline or compliance requirement [in India] against which it can be checked. "

Incoming surge

As organised and vocal as Delhi's rickshaw drivers may be, they are far outnumbered by the city's motorcycles and scooters.

With the ban on new non-electric two-wheeled vehicles starting in April 2028, the countdown is on to prepare the electrical grid for a surge in charging.

ICCT's Mr Bhatt said the smaller size of two- and three-wheeled EVs would make the transition easier for Delhi's infrastructure but admitted that access to chargers would be an obstacle for many.

Electric rickshaw drivers have reported technical issues at swappable battery charge points in Delhi. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

"Two-wheelers and three-wheelers do not require the massive public charging which a truck or a bus or even a car would require; a lot of charging will happen at home," Mr Bhatt said.

However, he conceded that after owning an EV himself for four years in Delhi, he still hadn't been permitted to install a charger at his home.

"My resident welfare association is saying, 'What if it catches fire because there is no [regulation or guidelines] on how to go about setting up this charging?'" he said.

This Delhi public charger listed four batteries as ready but then said none were available when a request was made. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Driver Indrajeet Sachdeva estimated 90 per cent of rickshaw owners did not have a space at home to install chargers.

At one of Delhi's public charging stations for swappable batteries, the ABC watched drivers waiting while the machine's display listed four batteries were ready.

When a battery was requested from the machine, a pop-up message said none were available.

Mr Sachdeva said issues like this meant the government needed to give the industry more time before going all-in on electrification.

Delhi's chief minister's office did not respond to a request for comment.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Blues, Magpies wildcard match hangs in balance as Dogs lead Dees but lose Naughton to injury
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury will miss Collingwood’s cutthroat wildcard final next week and could well have played his final match in black and white.

The Magpies revealed on Saturday that the VFL/AFL games-record holder had suffered a hamstring strain in the club’s loss to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Friday night, ruling him out for “two to three weeks”.

In a further blow to Collingwood, rugged defender Brayden Maynard strained the MCL in his left knee during a Saturday-morning training session and will also likely miss several weeks.

The Pendlebury injury will leave coach Craig McRae lamenting a decision to play his veteran leader in a match that ultimately had no bearing on their ladder position. Many felt he should have rested the former skipper.

“These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden,” Magpies head of football Charlie Gardiner said on Saturday afternoon.

“Scott experienced tightness in the back of his knee during last night’s game. Scans earlier today confirmed a hamstring strain, and we expect Scott to be sidelined for two to three weeks.

“Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade one MCL strain. This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury.

“These are unfortunate setbacks, especially at this time of year but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible.”

World.title: Can Australia afford to take Labuschagne back to the land of his birth?
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Can Australia afford to take Labuschagne back to the land of his birth? Daniel Brettig August 22, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Close your eyes, feel the sea breeze on your face and smell the barbecued snags wafting across the ground, and Australia’s second Test against Bangladesh could almost be a stand-in for their first against South Africa. Kingsmead in Durban, on South Africa’s eastern coast, is a good deal larger than Great Barrier Reef Arena, but its environs are not a million miles from Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne’s wretched run of form continues. Getty Images From the point Mitchell Starc cut the Bangladesh top order to pieces with 6-12, and certainly once the recalled Shoriful Islam (6-35) gave a fine impersonation of Marco Jansen to keep the tourists in the game, it was hard not to start thinking of the long-awaited trip to meet the Proteas in October. The dilemma for Australia right now is whether they can reasonably take the Klerksdorp-born Marnus Labuschagne across the Indian Ocean to enjoy the braai. On current evidence, he looks likely to be easy meat for Jansen, Kagiso Rabada, and Lungi Ngidi.



Before this game, coach Andrew McDonald and captain Pat Cummins played public bad cop and good cop with Labuschagne. McDonald stressed that he needed “big runs” in the aftermath of Australia’s surprising defeat in Darwin. Cummins then wrapped a rhetorical arm around Labuschagne by trying a version of the advice that appears to have worked for Cameron Green (51 not out), who made an overdue hundred last week and played fluently again here. Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Never let him settle’: Spin legend Mushie on Warne, Lyon and how Bangladesh humbled Australia “As a bowler, it feels like the margins are really small when someone like Marnus or Steve [Smith] are at their best form,” Cummins had said. “I’ve felt that the last couple of months. “Last week was a bit of a blip. Our message to Marnus is, ‘You don’t need to reinvent the wheel after last week’. Trust the work that he’s put in the last six months, because I think he’s in a really good place.” The “blip” grew larger on Saturday afternoon, as Shoriful gave a good approximation of the questions Jansen might ask in Durban and proved be beyond the capacity of Labuschagne, Travis Head or Smith to counter.



Head has some thinking to do as well, after dragging one on for the third time in as many innings, but he has many more credits in the bank than Labuschagne, whose streak of lowish scores is now stretching longer than many whole Test careers have done. Loading Without a hundred since the Old Trafford Ashes Test in 2023, Labuschagne may well not bat again in this game, and there will be no Sheffield Shield games before the selectors sit down to choose their white- and red-ball squads for South Africa. Always energetic, always thinking and always tinkering, Labuschagne seems unable to slow his mind down enough to return to the "zone" he enjoyed while churning out big scores consistently between 2019 and 2023. Concentration issues and mental mistakes were central to the selectors’ thinking when they dropped Labuschagne in the West Indies last year, and it was hoped a strong run of Shield scores leading into the Ashes last summer had helped him regain equilibrium.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection? But with each low score and each new way to get out, this time losing leg stump via the protruding bottom of his thigh pad, Labuschagne has been unable to stop himself from making continual adjustments, even in the nets this week. There’s an argument to be made that he is struggling to remember what his best method actually looks like. Simon Katich and Justin Langer, two former players with plenty of time for Labuschagne, sounded genuinely pained when trying to pin down the issues they could see from the Seven commentary box. It was left to their skipper Ricky Ponting to distil things. “The worry that I had with him ... I think he’s making the margin for error for the bowlers too great,” Ponting said. “With the length he can’t score off the back foot. He can’t score off the back foot in Test cricket. Batting becomes a hard game. “That’s the great difference between when he was at his best, and we highlighted some graphics earlier though you know three or four years ago where he’s averaging 65-68 for a Test year. That was when he was scoring off front foot and back foot.



“I think the bowlers now know that they can run in and bowl anywhere from almost 10 metres to about four metres on off stump and out as wide as they want, and he can’t hurt them. So I well and truly think it’s time to have a look at somebody else.” In the eight years since Australia's infamous previous Test tour to South Africa, cricket has got demonstrably harder for batsmen. Loading The Kookaburra ball is hardier, the pitches are greener and bowlers are only getting fitter and more precise. Over that time, Labuschagne's story has been a beguiling one, of a hard worker with enough talent to get to the top at a time when Australia needed him. The biggest concern for the selectors may be that, having already brought him back from the outer once, doing so again would look a lot like the end of the line. And they have already jettisoned one member of the top three, Jake Weatherald, this week.



It would indeed be a sad irony if an immigrant from South Africa is unable to return to play Test cricket there. But as the wickets kept tumbling in Mackay, 18 in total, Australia’s leaders were left only with uncomfortable questions. World.title: Autumn Glow outshines Sheza Alibi to win Winx Stakes as beaten owner eyes rematch
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Autumn Glow outshines Sheza Alibi to win Winx Stakes as beaten owner eyes rematch Craig Kerry August 22, 2026 — 6:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sheza Alibi owner Fred Noffke was looking forward to a potential rematch with Autumn Glow over a longer trip after his mare went down to the Chris Waller-trained star in round one of their rivalry on Saturday in the group 1 Winx Stakes (1400m) at Randwick. The clash of the glamour mares in the first group 1 of the season was the headline act, and it lived up to the hype as Autumn Glow bounced back from her first defeat, in the 2000m Queen Elizabeth Stakes in April, to beat Sheza Alibi by one and a half lengths. Autumn Glow surges to the lead, with Sheza Alibi, right, chasing. Getty Images James McDonald had five-year-old Autumn Glow ($1.75) a dream running line spot in fourth from gate three and she took over from leader Midnight Dynamite at the 200m and stole a gap. Sheza Alibi ($3.50), debuting in weight-for-age company, was slow away from barrier one but made up ground quickly to travel four back on the fence. The Doncaster and Randwick Guineas winner followed Autumn Glow into clear air late but could not make up the ground.



Noffke, who bought Sheza Alibi for $10,000 online as a weanling, was proud of the effort. “We got a bit more pushed and shoved about, lost a bit of momentum, but overall, yeah, it’s a very strong run,” Noffke said of the Peter Moody and Katherine Coleman-trained four-year-old. James McDonald celebrates after booting Autumn Glow home to victory. Getty Images “The 1400 is maybe a tad [short], against such company, but she beat everybody else over 1400, so in the end we’re incredibly proud. Peter was very happy, and Luke was very happy with the run.” He was looking forward to a potential clash at a mile, where he said Sheza Alibi was world class. That might not come, if Autumn Glow goes towards the 1200m $20 million Everest on October 17, rather than stretching to the mile. That decision will be made in the coming week.



For now, Autumn Glow part-owner and Arrowfield Stud founder John Messara was just relieved and proud of his star after a fourth group 1 win and 12th victory in 13 starts. “She hadn’t raced a lot of these horses before, so there was a bit of an unknown, and I respect the Victorian filly and I respect Peter Moody as a trainer, he’s no mug, so if he’s coming down, he gives himself a chance,” Messara said. “Running 1:21.03, it’s a fantastic time, so it was a proper test, she came through OK … I think she’s done enough, hasn’t she?” It was a 10th win for Waller in the race named after his legendary mare. “We’ve come out of round one pretty well,” he said of the Sheza Alibi showdown. “I’m sure there’s going to be a round two and three. Peter might make it a best of five.”



Related Article Horse racing Gollan filly makes flying return to cast shadow over spring features As for going to the Everest, where they would face defending champion Ka Ying Rising, Waller said: ”We might be wishing we were racing Sheza Alibi, if we go to the Everest.” Nash Rawiller picked up a surprise ride on Aeliana after his original booking, stablemate Beiwacht, was scratched on race morning because of a minor temperature. Aeliana, which finished last, was without a jockey all week and expected to be saved for the Memsie Stakes next week at Caulfield, where Beiwacht will now likely head. Waller also scratched Autumn Boy and Barnavara from the Winx. Waller was questioned by stewards about the late declaration of Rawiller to ride Aeliana and fined him $500. He told stewards Autumn Boy would instead run in the Memsie.

World.title: Swans launch a review of how Bloods culture crumbled in late-night party
World.content:
Sydney will launch a thorough review into the playing culture of their men’s team to work out how their famed Bloods culture has disintegrated. The Swans say they will leave no stone unturned into working out how standards within the dressing room crumbled to the point where five players were suspended for the rest of the season after a wild night of partying led to a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich and chairman Andrew Pridham fronted the media on Wednesday. George Chan “No culture is perfect,” Swans chairman Andrew Pridham told this masthead on Saturday. “We have never said it is. Clearly we need to look into what went wrong. The standards we set were not the problem. It is that they were breached. We need to understand why this happened. We will do this thoroughly.”



The Swans will take on North Melbourne on Sunday in their final game of the home-and-away season, after a week in which Pridham said the club-imposed sanctions would “torpedo” Sydney’s premiership hopes. The saga deepened on Saturday as a woman who alleges she was the victim of a sexual assault during the late-night party in a Melbourne hotel room hired a lawyer to prepare civil legal action. Law firm Slater and Gordon confirmed it had been engaged to investigate a potential civil claim on behalf of the woman, as lawyer Jackson Pannam said she was “trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience”. The Pullman East Melbourne hotel, where the Swans players stayed on Sunday night. Simon Schluter He said his client called the police “immediately after what had happened” in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman East hotel.



“She’s provided a statement, and she’s continuing to assist the police with their investigation,” Pannam said. Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Nobody knows if any of these five will play for the Swans again “Whatever the outcome of the criminal investigation, we intend to explore other avenues for our clients to seek justice, including through civil remedies. We will be putting all of the relevant parties on notice in due course.” Pannam told reporters the woman’s complaint to police was about “alleged sexual assaults”. A police spokesperson, in a statement on Saturday morning, said Sexual Crimes Squad detectives continued “to investigate a report of a sexual assault”.



“The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established and a number of people have been spoken to,” the spokesperson said. “As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken.” This masthead has previously reported that star player Isaac Heeney is at the centre of the police inquiry. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine Five Swans players – Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were stood down for the rest of the season for breaching the club’s standards.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL off-field behaviour Swans hotel drama deepens as former star placed inside late-night party On Friday, a lawyer representing the other two women who were present at the hotel on Monday described what occurred as “demeaning, abhorrent and simply not moral or acceptable”. “These women were subjected to the most disgusting actions and behaviour I have ever heard about in my 28 years as a lawyer,” Carbone Lawyers head of personal injury and litigation John Karantzis told 3AW. Karantzis also claimed there were “even a few leaders in that room” along with the five Swans players. Pannam described those comments as unhelpful, and said the woman he represented wanted privacy.



“I’m not in the business of ranking the types of cases that I’ve been involved in,” he said. “Certainly, I don’t think that’s helpful.” The Swans have denied there were any other club officials or staff members in the hotel room. “The Sydney Swans supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today’s statement regarding the investigation,” the club said on Saturday. Loading



“The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation.



“The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage.” Pannam, when asked who his client intended to launch legal action against, said: “A claim for compensation can be made against anyone who has caused or contributed to someone suffering injury, harm, damage. It’s very early days, and we are considering our options. “We’ll be writing to the relevant parties in due course with a view to putting them on notice of what our intentions are.” One of the women, speaking on a podcast recorded before last weekend’s events, described how as a younger sex worker, she had dealt with people expecting that if they were paying for a service, they could treat her a certain way, or who would go into strip clubs to mess with the heads of women working there. World.title: ‘People like me don’t have babies’: Inside the clinic helping addicted expectant mums
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Elvira was in the grip of a heroin addiction when she found out she was pregnant with her first child. “I thought, ‘People like me don’t have babies,’” Elvira says. “I shouldn’t be a mum.” Elvira beat a heroin addiction. Now, she works with expectant mums as a peer support leader at Western Health’s Sapphire Clinic. Justin McManus Elvira is not a religious person, but she likens a heroin addiction to being possessed by the devil: an unstoppable, violent force that drags a person into hell against their will. She remembers crying on the way to her dealer’s house, desperate to stop using. “No one will ever carry as much shame and judgment about ourselves as mothers in addiction,” Elvira, who asked for her surname to be withheld for privacy reasons, says. “No one will ever judge or shame us as much as we do ourselves. We don’t want to be doing it.” The 50-year-old mother of two, who has bipolar II and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), has been clean for more than eight years.



Related Article Coronavirus pandemic Debra knows how post-natal anxiety feels, now she's helping other mums Now Elvira works with expectant mums as a peer support leader at Western Health’s Sapphire Clinic. The pioneering antenatal and multidisciplinary health clinic at the Joan Kirner Women and Children’s Hospital in St Albans has been running for more than a year. So far, it has helped more than 130 women during their pregnancies with trauma-informed, non-judgmental healthcare spanning from addiction medicine to obstetrics, midwifery, perinatal psychological support, maternal-fetal monitoring, infectious diseases, dietetics and social work. Many of the women who come into the clinic are just like Tsecoutanis once was: in the throes of addiction, homeless, sleeping in their cars, or battling complex mental health conditions. Others are desperate to get into rehab so they can kick the drugs or alcohol to get sober for their babies. “I see the same shame and wariness in them that I felt inside myself,” Elvira says. “Drugs are illegal, right? They are so judged on a moral level, so there’s this barrier immediately.” Elvira tells the women her own story about drug and alcohol use, fleeing violent relationships, of raising her two young children, of falling in and out of addiction for years until she finally stopped.



“So many of them have so much trauma,” she says. “I can see them relax a little bit and then slowly they start to open up because they know I understand.” Related Article Australian music ‘I didn’t care if I lived or died’: Charlie Collins on the addiction that nearly destroyed her It is a Friday morning inside the brightly lit hospital clinic. The phone at the front desk barely stops ringing, and associate midwife unit manager Kylie Charles is working with military precision. She is making welfare calls to women at home and ensuring all their appointments with specialists are booked for the same day, with minimum waiting time. “It can be really hard for some of these women to get here, so we want to make it as easy as possible for them,” she says. Nearby, a young pregnant woman is FaceTiming her father in the waiting area, while another woman sits quietly in a plastic chair, grey hooded jumper pulled over head, eyes downcast, hands resting on her swollen belly. They are waiting to see GP and addiction medicine specialist Dr Thileepan Naren. Years of working in regional Victoria with Indigenous communities have instilled in him a calling to reduce the prejudice and shame of getting healthcare while grappling with addiction.



Addiction medicine specialist Dr Thileepan Naren. Justin McManus “A lot of the women I am seeing are used to being judged, or stigmatised, or treated poorly,” he says. “Often they don’t feel like they deserve care at all, so it’s about trying to fight against that misconception and say, ‘No, we’re here to support you and your baby.’” Related Article Exclusive

Drugs Surge in women using date-rape substance as party drug leads to spike in hospitalisations Sometimes, the first step is finding a safe place for them to live. “There have been cases where we’ve had patients who have come in and been in quite dire straits, whether it be with significant domestic violence or homelessness,” he says. Others are withdrawing from heroin, methamphetamine, alcohol or nitrous oxide and need help getting into detox or rehabilitation programs.



Increasingly, clinicians are supporting a complex cohort of pregnant patients addicted to GHB, also known as liquid ecstasy. Related Article Motherhood Ellen wished to go to hospital, just for a rest. She wants you to know this about mums’ mental health Weaning off the drug is “like alcohol withdrawal on steroids”, Naren says. It can trigger a fast-moving storm in the brain and body, which can lead to spikes in heart rate and blood pressure. In the most serious cases, they end up in intensive care. Obstetrician Andrea Walker instigated setting up the clinic after noticing there were gaps in the antenatal care being provided to women in the western suburbs. World.title: AFL LIVE: Blues, Magpies wildcard match hangs in balance as Dogs lead Dees but lose Naughton to injury
World.content:
Scott Pendlebury will miss Collingwood’s cutthroat wildcard final next week and could well have played his final match in black and white.

The Magpies revealed on Saturday that the VFL/AFL games-record holder had suffered a hamstring strain in the club’s loss to the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Friday night, ruling him out for “two to three weeks”.

In a further blow to Collingwood, rugged defender Brayden Maynard strained the MCL in his left knee during a Saturday-morning training session and will also likely miss several weeks.

The Pendlebury injury will leave coach Craig McRae lamenting a decision to play his veteran leader in a match that ultimately had no bearing on their ladder position. Many felt he should have rested the former skipper.

“These are obviously disappointing setbacks for both Scott and Brayden,” Magpies head of football Charlie Gardiner said on Saturday afternoon.

“Scott experienced tightness in the back of his knee during last night’s game. Scans earlier today confirmed a hamstring strain, and we expect Scott to be sidelined for two to three weeks.

“Brayden unfortunately left the track early this morning during a training session, with scans confirming he sustained a grade one MCL strain. This is the same knee but unrelated to his earlier injury.

“These are unfortunate setbacks, especially at this time of year but Scott and Brayden are absolute professionals and will do all they can to get back as quickly as possible.”

World.title: Can Australia afford to take Labuschagne back to the land of his birth?
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Can Australia afford to take Labuschagne back to the land of his birth? Daniel Brettig August 22, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Close your eyes, feel the sea breeze on your face and smell the barbecued snags wafting across the ground, and Australia’s second Test against Bangladesh could almost be a stand-in for their first against South Africa. Kingsmead in Durban, on South Africa’s eastern coast, is a good deal larger than Great Barrier Reef Arena, but its environs are not a million miles from Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne’s wretched run of form continues. Getty Images From the point Mitchell Starc cut the Bangladesh top order to pieces with 6-12, and certainly once the recalled Shoriful Islam (6-35) gave a fine impersonation of Marco Jansen to keep the tourists in the game, it was hard not to start thinking of the long-awaited trip to meet the Proteas in October. The dilemma for Australia right now is whether they can reasonably take the Klerksdorp-born Marnus Labuschagne across the Indian Ocean to enjoy the braai. On current evidence, he looks likely to be easy meat for Jansen, Kagiso Rabada, and Lungi Ngidi.



Before this game, coach Andrew McDonald and captain Pat Cummins played public bad cop and good cop with Labuschagne. McDonald stressed that he needed “big runs” in the aftermath of Australia’s surprising defeat in Darwin. Cummins then wrapped a rhetorical arm around Labuschagne by trying a version of the advice that appears to have worked for Cameron Green (51 not out), who made an overdue hundred last week and played fluently again here. Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Never let him settle’: Spin legend Mushie on Warne, Lyon and how Bangladesh humbled Australia “As a bowler, it feels like the margins are really small when someone like Marnus or Steve [Smith] are at their best form,” Cummins had said. “I’ve felt that the last couple of months. “Last week was a bit of a blip. Our message to Marnus is, ‘You don’t need to reinvent the wheel after last week’. Trust the work that he’s put in the last six months, because I think he’s in a really good place.” The “blip” grew larger on Saturday afternoon, as Shoriful gave a good approximation of the questions Jansen might ask in Durban and proved be beyond the capacity of Labuschagne, Travis Head or Smith to counter.



Head has some thinking to do as well, after dragging one on for the third time in as many innings, but he has many more credits in the bank than Labuschagne, whose streak of lowish scores is now stretching longer than many whole Test careers have done. Loading Without a hundred since the Old Trafford Ashes Test in 2023, Labuschagne may well not bat again in this game, and there will be no Sheffield Shield games before the selectors sit down to choose their white- and red-ball squads for South Africa. Always energetic, always thinking and always tinkering, Labuschagne seems unable to slow his mind down enough to return to the "zone" he enjoyed while churning out big scores consistently between 2019 and 2023. Concentration issues and mental mistakes were central to the selectors’ thinking when they dropped Labuschagne in the West Indies last year, and it was hoped a strong run of Shield scores leading into the Ashes last summer had helped him regain equilibrium.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection? But with each low score and each new way to get out, this time losing leg stump via the protruding bottom of his thigh pad, Labuschagne has been unable to stop himself from making continual adjustments, even in the nets this week. There’s an argument to be made that he is struggling to remember what his best method actually looks like. Simon Katich and Justin Langer, two former players with plenty of time for Labuschagne, sounded genuinely pained when trying to pin down the issues they could see from the Seven commentary box. It was left to their skipper Ricky Ponting to distil things. “The worry that I had with him ... I think he’s making the margin for error for the bowlers too great,” Ponting said. “With the length he can’t score off the back foot. He can’t score off the back foot in Test cricket. Batting becomes a hard game. “That’s the great difference between when he was at his best, and we highlighted some graphics earlier though you know three or four years ago where he’s averaging 65-68 for a Test year. That was when he was scoring off front foot and back foot.



“I think the bowlers now know that they can run in and bowl anywhere from almost 10 metres to about four metres on off stump and out as wide as they want, and he can’t hurt them. So I well and truly think it’s time to have a look at somebody else.” In the eight years since Australia's infamous previous Test tour to South Africa, cricket has got demonstrably harder for batsmen. Loading The Kookaburra ball is hardier, the pitches are greener and bowlers are only getting fitter and more precise. Over that time, Labuschagne's story has been a beguiling one, of a hard worker with enough talent to get to the top at a time when Australia needed him. The biggest concern for the selectors may be that, having already brought him back from the outer once, doing so again would look a lot like the end of the line. And they have already jettisoned one member of the top three, Jake Weatherald, this week.



It would indeed be a sad irony if an immigrant from South Africa is unable to return to play Test cricket there. But as the wickets kept tumbling in Mackay, 18 in total, Australia’s leaders were left only with uncomfortable questions.
