World.title: Autumn Glow outshines Sheza Alibi to win Winx Stakes as beaten owner eyes rematch
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Autumn Glow outshines Sheza Alibi to win Winx Stakes as beaten owner eyes rematch Craig Kerry August 22, 2026 — 6:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sheza Alibi owner Fred Noffke was looking forward to a potential rematch with Autumn Glow over a longer trip after his mare went down to the Chris Waller-trained star in round one of their rivalry on Saturday in the group 1 Winx Stakes (1400m) at Randwick. The clash of the glamour mares in the first group 1 of the season was the headline act, and it lived up to the hype as Autumn Glow bounced back from her first defeat, in the 2000m Queen Elizabeth Stakes in April, to beat Sheza Alibi by one and a half lengths. Autumn Glow surges to the lead, with Sheza Alibi, right, chasing. Getty Images James McDonald had five-year-old Autumn Glow ($1.75) a dream running line spot in fourth from gate three and she took over from leader Midnight Dynamite at the 200m and stole a gap. Sheza Alibi ($3.50), debuting in weight-for-age company, was slow away from barrier one but made up ground quickly to travel four back on the fence. The Doncaster and Randwick Guineas winner followed Autumn Glow into clear air late but could not make up the ground.



Noffke, who bought Sheza Alibi for $10,000 online as a weanling, was proud of the effort. “We got a bit more pushed and shoved about, lost a bit of momentum, but overall, yeah, it’s a very strong run,” Noffke said of the Peter Moody and Katherine Coleman-trained four-year-old. James McDonald celebrates after booting Autumn Glow home to victory. Getty Images “The 1400 is maybe a tad [short], against such company, but she beat everybody else over 1400, so in the end we’re incredibly proud. Peter was very happy, and Luke was very happy with the run.” He was looking forward to a potential clash at a mile, where he said Sheza Alibi was world class. That might not come, if Autumn Glow goes towards the 1200m $20 million Everest on October 17, rather than stretching to the mile. That decision will be made in the coming week.



For now, Autumn Glow part-owner and Arrowfield Stud founder John Messara was just relieved and proud of his star after a fourth group 1 win and 12th victory in 13 starts. “She hadn’t raced a lot of these horses before, so there was a bit of an unknown, and I respect the Victorian filly and I respect Peter Moody as a trainer, he’s no mug, so if he’s coming down, he gives himself a chance,” Messara said. “Running 1:21.03, it’s a fantastic time, so it was a proper test, she came through OK … I think she’s done enough, hasn’t she?” It was a 10th win for Waller in the race named after his legendary mare. “We’ve come out of round one pretty well,” he said of the Sheza Alibi showdown. “I’m sure there’s going to be a round two and three. Peter might make it a best of five.”



Related Article Horse racing Gollan filly makes flying return to cast shadow over spring features As for going to the Everest, where they would face defending champion Ka Ying Rising, Waller said: ”We might be wishing we were racing Sheza Alibi, if we go to the Everest.” Nash Rawiller picked up a surprise ride on Aeliana after his original booking, stablemate Beiwacht, was scratched on race morning because of a minor temperature. Aeliana, which finished last, was without a jockey all week and expected to be saved for the Memsie Stakes next week at Caulfield, where Beiwacht will now likely head. Waller also scratched Autumn Boy and Barnavara from the Winx. Waller was questioned by stewards about the late declaration of Rawiller to ride Aeliana and fined him $500. He told stewards Autumn Boy would instead run in the Memsie.

World.title: Swans launch a review of how Bloods culture crumbled in late-night party
World.content:
Sydney will launch a thorough review into the playing culture of their men’s team to work out how their famed Bloods culture has disintegrated. The Swans say they will leave no stone unturned into working out how standards within the dressing room crumbled to the point where five players were suspended for the rest of the season after a wild night of partying led to a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich and chairman Andrew Pridham fronted the media on Wednesday. George Chan “No culture is perfect,” Swans chairman Andrew Pridham told this masthead on Saturday. “We have never said it is. Clearly we need to look into what went wrong. The standards we set were not the problem. It is that they were breached. We need to understand why this happened. We will do this thoroughly.”



The Swans will take on North Melbourne on Sunday in their final game of the home-and-away season, after a week in which Pridham said the club-imposed sanctions would “torpedo” Sydney’s premiership hopes. The saga deepened on Saturday as a woman who alleges she was the victim of a sexual assault during the late-night party in a Melbourne hotel room hired a lawyer to prepare civil legal action. Law firm Slater and Gordon confirmed it had been engaged to investigate a potential civil claim on behalf of the woman, as lawyer Jackson Pannam said she was “trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience”. The Pullman East Melbourne hotel, where the Swans players stayed on Sunday night. Simon Schluter He said his client called the police “immediately after what had happened” in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman East hotel.



“She’s provided a statement, and she’s continuing to assist the police with their investigation,” Pannam said. Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Nobody knows if any of these five will play for the Swans again “Whatever the outcome of the criminal investigation, we intend to explore other avenues for our clients to seek justice, including through civil remedies. We will be putting all of the relevant parties on notice in due course.” Pannam told reporters the woman’s complaint to police was about “alleged sexual assaults”. A police spokesperson, in a statement on Saturday morning, said Sexual Crimes Squad detectives continued “to investigate a report of a sexual assault”.



“The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established and a number of people have been spoken to,” the spokesperson said. “As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken.” This masthead has previously reported that star player Isaac Heeney is at the centre of the police inquiry. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine Five Swans players – Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were stood down for the rest of the season for breaching the club’s standards.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL off-field behaviour Swans hotel drama deepens as former star placed inside late-night party On Friday, a lawyer representing the other two women who were present at the hotel on Monday described what occurred as “demeaning, abhorrent and simply not moral or acceptable”. “These women were subjected to the most disgusting actions and behaviour I have ever heard about in my 28 years as a lawyer,” Carbone Lawyers head of personal injury and litigation John Karantzis told 3AW. Karantzis also claimed there were “even a few leaders in that room” along with the five Swans players. Pannam described those comments as unhelpful, and said the woman he represented wanted privacy.



“I’m not in the business of ranking the types of cases that I’ve been involved in,” he said. “Certainly, I don’t think that’s helpful.” The Swans have denied there were any other club officials or staff members in the hotel room. “The Sydney Swans supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today’s statement regarding the investigation,” the club said on Saturday. Loading



“The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation.



“The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage.” Pannam, when asked who his client intended to launch legal action against, said: “A claim for compensation can be made against anyone who has caused or contributed to someone suffering injury, harm, damage. It’s very early days, and we are considering our options. “We’ll be writing to the relevant parties in due course with a view to putting them on notice of what our intentions are.” One of the women, speaking on a podcast recorded before last weekend’s events, described how as a younger sex worker, she had dealt with people expecting that if they were paying for a service, they could treat her a certain way, or who would go into strip clubs to mess with the heads of women working there. World.title: Three hurt in Lindis Pass crash
World.content:
Police are seeking witnesses after three people have been critically injured following a crash on Lindis Pass.

Emergency services were called to State Highway 8, between Lindis Pass-Tarras Road and Birchwood Road, at about 7.40am on Saturday.

Oamaru Police Sergeant Tony Woodbridge said two vehicles were involved in the crash, which happened near Dalrachney Station.

On Saturday evening Woodbridge gave an update: "Three people were transported to hospital, where they remain in critical condition, and our thoughts are with their families at this extremely difficult time".

The Omarama-Lindis Pass Road had reopened after it was closed for several hours after the crash while a scene examination was carried out, but police were still seeking more information, he said.

"Police would like to hear from anyone who witnessed the crash or who might have dashcam footage of it.

"In particular, Police are hoping to speak with a man we believe witnessed the crash and was one of the first people on scene.

"He left before Police arrived, and we are hoping he will come forward and speak with us to help us build a picture of what occurred."

Woodbridge also thanked the people who stopped at the scene of the crash to help and carry out first aid on the injured.

World.title: Police investigate Far North death
World.content:
A woman has been arrested and police have launched an investigation, after a man's death in the Far North.

Emergency services were called to a property in Haruru, near Paihia, about 4.30am Saturday, where a man was unresponsive, police said.

He was pronounced dead a short time later.

Northland Detective Inspector Rhys Johnston said the mean's death was unexplained and a 56-year-old woman was arrested at the scene.

"She has been charged with assault," Johnston said.

Enquiries were underway to find out how the man died.

A post mortem would be carried out on Sunday and a scene guard was in place.

The community could expect to see an increased police presence in the area.

World.title: Auckland City FC bag 14th Oceania Champions League crown
World.content:
Auckland City have won a fifth successive men's Oceania Champions League crown and a 14th in a total after beating Solomon Islands club Central Coast FC 2-0 in the final in Fiji.

Second half goals to Ryan De Vries and Matt Ellis proved the difference in humid conditions at Govind Park in Ba.

A tight first half was followed by a tense start to the second spell before the New Zealand side broke through, when Michal Doudera's stinging shot from the edge of the penalty area was parried by the goalkeeper into the path of De Vries, who tapped home.

The second goal came nine minutes after the first.

Substitute Ryan Watson burst down the right flank and cut infield before a pinpoint cross picked out a sliding Ellis.

Central Coast FC's hopes of a comeback were dealt a further blow in the 83rd minute when Prince Tahunipue was shown a straight red card for his part in a confrontation.

The decider came 10 days after the same two clubs played the tournament's opening game, in which Auckland City needed two late goals to prevail 2-1, with club great De Vries again finding the net.

The Navy Blues have now won all 14 finals they've contested in the 24-year history of the amateur-based OFC Champions League

World.title: 'Hoping for the best': How a police officer was left fighting for his life after a car struck him
World.content:
A police officer is in a critical condition in Wellington Hospital after he was struck by a car, allegedly stolen in Palmerston North, and thrown several metres. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports on what is known so far.

It was about 2am on Saturday when a Palmerston North-based constable decided to use some road spikes in an attempt to stop what was believed to be a stolen car.

The officer, who has been in the police for less than two years, was behind his police car as he prepared to use the spikes at a driveway.

Moments later the car he was trying to stop travelled down Kairanga Bunnythorpe Rd in Manawatū on the wrong side of the road.

Police say the driver, a teenager, managed to avoid the spikes before striking a car, shunting it out of the way, and hitting two police officers.

One of the officers, described as a "fantastic young man", was thrown several metres into the side of a car parked in the drive. His colleague suffered minor injuries.

The critically injured officer, who is a father to a toddler, is now on a ventilator at Wellington Hospital, surrounded by his family.

A 14-year-old and 15-year-old are in custody and a police critical incident investigation is underway, with the Independent Police Conduct Authority also notified.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the incident was "driven by two young people".

"They've stolen a car, and they've made a decision. I don't know based on what.

"However, we're responding to their actions and I think that we, in this instance, did all that we could a) to try and apprehend them in the first instance, and then b) avoid this, which is the worst outcome."

Driver allegedly fled from police

Bennett said the driver of the car was signalled to stop about 2am on Amberley Avenue, but allegedly fled.

"Police followed the vehicle initially, and as that vehicle sped away, police withdrew from that pursuit.

"It was on a long, straight stretch of road and our officers, who know the area very well, were some way down that road and took a vantage point and decided they would use it to deploy spikes."

The officer was positioned behind his police car while preparing to deploy the spikes at a driveway between Rongotea Rd and Gillespies Line.

Bennett said the car was travelling eastbound on the wrong side of the road when it struck the police car, and then the two officers.

"At the time that they were struck, they had just deployed spikes to stop the stolen vehicle.

"The stolen vehicle was travelling at such a speed that it avoided the spikes or swerved to avoid the spikes, struck a police car, shunted the police car out of the way, and went on to strike the other officers."

The officer's colleague immediately provided support to him while other staff responded to the scene.

The officer was flown to Wellington Hospital, arriving about 4am "in spite of challenging weather conditions", Bennett said.

Two youths were arrested at the scene.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett speaks to media after a police officer was hit in Palmerston North. NZ Police

Officer's family 'extremely thankful' to responders

Speaking to media on Saturday afternoon, Bennett said the officer remained in a critical condition in Wellington Hospital with his family beside him.

"He's on a ventilator, and it's a matter of time and waiting until such time as the medical team can make further assessments and give us a prognosis. That time may not be as soon as we hope for."

Bennett said the officer's family had asked him to acknowledge those who responded to the incident.

"On behalf of the family, I'd like to say thank you to firstly our officer's immediate colleagues who were on scene with him, whose immediate actions certainly have been beneficial to the first responders and to the flight teams that got him here, they're extremely thankful to them and the medical teams that are working with him now. So, on behalf of the family, we say thank you."

Asked whether the incident appeared to be "targeted", Bennett said that would form part of the investigation.

"But there's nothing that initial examination would say it was intentional. However, there's interviews with the suspects to complete, there's a scene examination, as you can imagine, which will take some time and be thorough."

Bennett did not know how fast the stolen car was travelling at this time, and said it was too early to say what charges the teens would be facing.

The incident occurred in Palmerston North at 2am on Saturday. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

He said the officer was a young father.

"Him and his partner have a young toddler, and he comes from a very strong family, who are service-orientated. They describe him as having a deep soul for a young man, and importantly, in their words, 'he's a good bloke'.

"He's the type of person that you want to sit down and have a conversation with, and certainly in his career, his short career as a police officer, he graduated in December 2024… he certainly proved to be that."

Bennett said police were "extremely grateful the outcome was not worse".

"That is thanks to the efforts of those who responded. The officers' colleagues were faced with an appalling situation and I'm incredibly proud of them," he said.

"Everyone went above and beyond to save a life last night, and it made the difference."

'We are humbled by the support'

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers visited the officer in Wellington Hospital on Saturday.

He praised the actions of the staff at the scene.

"Their response was fast and effective, and they provided the best care they could while ambulance staff got to the scene. No amount of training can prepare you for a situation where you are trying to save the life of a colleague and friend, and they acted with exceptional professionalism.

"This incident highlights the risk my staff face while doing their jobs to keep their communities safe and I would like to acknowledge the efforts of everyone involved last night."

Chambers is travelling to Palmerston North on Saturday evening to speak with the staff there.

"We are humbled by the support from members of the community and people across the country, and on behalf of my staff, I thank everyone who has sent kind messages of support."

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Police Minister Mark Mitchell earlier told RNZ he was travelling to Wellington to support the injured officer.

"The Commissioner and I will be providing any support that the family require," he said.

"Policing by its sheer nature does carry risk, there's no doubt about that, but of course that doesn't lessen or reduce the impact that is felt when one of our police officers is injured in the line of duty.

"They are out there protecting their community, they are representative of us, they do carry that risk, but it doesn't make it any easier when a police officer is seriously hurt, injured or killed."

The president of the Police Association, Steve Watt, said incidents like this were felt by all members.

"Ultimately, the police is a big family and when these sorts of things happen it really cuts deep and it affects us all," he said.

"Much like the rest of our members, we're waiting and hoping for the best outcome."

Watt said the association was working with police's welfare network and organising wrap around support, not only for the officer but for his family.

World.title: Warriors sign McFadden for long-haul
World.content:
The Warriors have further bolstered their NRL back office by extending the contract of the club's general manager for recruitment, pathways and development, Andrew McFadden.

A former Warriors head coach, McFadden has extended his decade-long commitment in Auckland by signing on for an "indefinite term".

It comes days after head coach Andrew Webster was confirmed as staying at the club until 2032.

Chief executive Cameron George was delighted to secure both signatures in quick succession.

Cameron George Photosport

"It's critical for us to have both Webby and Cappy committed long-term," he said.

"These announcements have been planned in my thinking for some time given we share the same vision and are aligned on the future shape of the New Zealand Warriors.

"Having stability in these critical roles will ultimately bring ongoing success.

"When we reset for our homecoming, Cappy's appointment was of the utmost importance to us. He is a passionate and dynamic contributor to our journey and we all value his opinion.

"What we are seeing the club achieve across the board now sheets back to what he and his staff put in place three years ago and have continued to shape."

The 48-year-old McFadden - a halfback for the Canberra Raiders in his playing days - spent six seasons at the Warriors from 2013-2018 as both head coach and assistant coach, before returning in late 2022.

"This role with the club has been incredibly rewarding. There's so much talent around New Zealand and we're seeing the results of the work everyone is doing," McFadden said.

World.title: Fleeing driver in Palmerston North leaves officer in critical condition
World.content:
A police officer remains in a critical condition after being hit by a fleeing driver in Palmerston North overnight.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the officer was a young father and known to be a "good bloke".

On Saturday afternoon he said the officer was still in critical condition and on a ventilator.

Bennett said the driver had been signalled to stop about 2am on Amberley Avenue but allegedly fled.

"Minutes later, the vehicle, which was not being pursued, hit a police officer laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road. The officer suffered critical injuries and was airlifted to Wellington Hospital, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries.

"The circumstances of what occurred remain under investigation. From our initial enquiries, the vehicle appeared to be stolen."

Bennett said the two young people who were arrested were 14 and 15 years old.

"After fleeing, the vehicle was monitored as it travelled out of the city. The officer was positioned behind his patrol car preparing to deploy spikes at a driveway between Rongotea Road and Gillespies Line," Superintendent Bennett said.

"The suspect vehicle was travelling eastbound on the wrong side of Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road when it struck the police vehicle, and then the two officers. The seriously injured officer was thrown into the side of a car that was parked in the drive."

The two youths were taken into custody at the scene.

Police are due to speak to the alleged offenders and charges are being considered, Bennett said.

The Police officer had been laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road when they were hit and injured. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers visited the injured officer in Wellington Hospital this afternoon and commended the police response.

"No amount of training can prepare you for a situation where you are trying to save the life of a colleague and friend, and they acted with exceptional professionalism.

"This incident highlights the risk my staff face while doing their jobs to keep their communities safe and I would like to acknowledge the efforts of everyone involved last night."

Chambers said he would be travelling to Palmerston North on Saturday evening to speak with the staff there and meet some of those involved in this incident

"We are humbled by the support from members of the community and people across the country, and on behalf of my staff, I thank everyone who has sent kind messages of support."

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The police critical incident investigation is ongoing, and the Independent Police Conduct Authority has been notified.

"We are extremely grateful the outcome was not worse and that is thanks to the efforts of those who responded. The officers' colleagues were faced with an appalling situation and I'm incredibly proud of them," Bennett said.

A scene examination was being carried out by the Serious Crash Unit and a section of the road remained closed.

Locals said that area had been plagued by serious accidents over many years.

A spokesperson for the Greater Bunnythorpe Committee, Mandy Shaw, said that while the officer was hit at the Kairanga end of Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road, the wider stretch of the road included some of the country's deadliest intersections.

She said the committee continued to advocate for meaningful safety improvements along the road, particularly given that most of it remains subject to a 100 kilometre per hour speed limit.

'Waiting and hoping for the best outcome'

Police Minister Mark Mitchell told RNZ he was travelling to Wellington to support the injured officer.

"The Commissioner and I will be providing any support that the family require," he said.

"Policing by its sheer nature does carry risk, there's no doubt about that, but of course that doesn't lessen or reduce the impact that is felt when one of our police officers is injured in the line of duty.

"They are out there protecting their community, they are representative of us, they do carry that risk, but it doesn't make it any easier when a police officer is seriously hurt, injured or killed."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

The president of the Police Association, Steve Watt, said family of the officer were by his bedside in hospital.

He said incidents like this were felt by all members.

"Ultimately, the police is a big family and when these sorts of things happen it really cuts deep and it affects us all," he said.

"Much like the rest of our members, we're waiting and hoping for the best outcome."

Watt said they were working with police's welfare network and organising wrap around support not only for the officer but for his family.

"There's a reasonably large contingent of family that have headed to Wellington, so we'll look to continue to support them and make sure that they're well looked after," he said.

The Police officer had been laying spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road when they were hit and injured. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Echoes of previous case

The injuring of the Palmerston North officer comes 18 years after Sergeant Derek Wootton was killed while laying road spikes in Porirua, north of Wellington.

The 52-year-old was working the night shift when a report was received of a serious assault and carjacking.

Police patrols saw the reported stolen Honda near Porirua and followed it to Titahi Bay. The Honda had reached speeds of 160km/h as it drove through residential streets. Wootton was struck by the car as he deployed the spikes at around 3am on Dimock Street in Titahi Bay. The impact propelled him nearly 30m down the road.

Wootton had previously worked as a builder and milkman before joining the police, and was first posted to Porirua as a constable when he graduated in 1994. Then-Wellington Police District Commander Pieri Munroe described him as an experienced frontline supervisor.

Andrew Popo, a 32-year-old Mongrel Mob member, was charged with dangerous driving, dangerous driving causing death and failing to stop after a motor accident. He was also charged with aggravated robbery, the theft of a Honda Prelude and kidnapping a 16-year-old. He was sentenced to eight years and nine months in jail for manslaughter.

Justice McKenzie says he took into account Popo's genuine remorse and his guilty plea to the manslaughter charge, but also noted a previous history of offending and gang connections.

World.title: Wallaroos hammered in historic 100th Test by ruthless Black Ferns
World.content:
The Wallaroos' 100th Test match, and the Test debut of Australia's all-time leading rugby 7s try-scorer, has been soured by a dominant New Zealand performance in Auckland.

The Black Ferns maintained their unblemished record against the Wallaroos in Test rugby, with a 66-19 win at Mt Smart Stadium.

New Zealand came into Saturday's Test having not lost to Australia in all 30 Tests between the two nations, and a 10-try haul ensured that streak would continue.

The Wallaroos scored three tries, including a score from Waiaria Ellis who started at fly half for the first time.

Maddison Levi, Australia's all-time leading rugby 7s try scorer, made her Wallaroos debut with a 30-minute stint off the bench. Meanwhile, Emily Chancellor became the first woman to represent the Black Ferns and Wallaroos in Test rugby when she made her Australian debut off the bench.

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said her team was disappointed in the result, but was pleased the Australians continued fighting, managing to score two of the game's final three tries.

"New Zealand started off really fast, so we were on the back foot," she said.

"But you could see towards the end that we can get back, it's just a matter of starting well."

Highlights were few and far between for the Wallaroos as the Black Ferns dominated from the opening whistle.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' As the Wallaroos prepare for their 100th Test, past and present players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching this milestone.

A brilliant counter ruck inside Australian territory gave the home side possession, and the Black Ferns then methodically worked their way to the goal-line before fullback Braxton Sorensen-McGee scored on the right flank in the fourth minute.

The Black Ferns continued their early dominance. The Wallaroos were forced to scramble on their goal line to hold out a rampant home side, with New Zealand lock Maiakawanakaulani Roos held up over the line from a line-out maul.

That was just a reprieve for the Wallaroos, as the Black Ferns continued to attack, with prop Chryss Viliko charging over from close range for the second try.

The Black Ferns had a third try in the 24th minute, with lock Maama Mo'onia Vaipulu making a big line break up the middle of the field before passing to fly half Ruahei Demant, who scored under the posts.

New Zealand's one blemish in the first half was Vaipulu being sent to the sin bin, not lowering herself enough in a tackle and making head-on-head contact with Wallaroos' flanker Lily Bone.

Being down to 14 women did not seem to matter to the Black Ferns, who scored a fourth try when Liana Mikaele-Tu'u touched down in the 35th minute.

The Wallaroos were able to take momentum into half-time with their first try of the afternoon. A free kick against the Black Ferns from their own line-out, gave the Wallaroos the ball near the opposition goal-line. The visitors seized the opportunity, with left winger Desiree Miller scoring and then converting her own try.

Down 26-7 at half-time, any hope the Wallaroos had of making a famous comeback was doused quickly.

After being held up early in the first half, Roos finished off a nice passage of play to score New Zealand's fifth try just three minutes into the second half.

By the time Australia's Rugby 7's all-time leading try scorer Levi came on for her Wallaroos debut, the game was not a contest.

Tries to Ayesha Leti-I'iga in the 50th minute and reserve hooker Vici-Rose Green in the 56th minute piled on more misery for the Wallaroos.

The Black Ferns crossed the half-century mark with a try to Maia Joseph, then Shyrah Tuliau-Tua'a charged down a kick from Wallaroos fullback Faitala Moleka inside the Australian in-goal, and grounded the ball.

A lovely side-step from Wallaroos fly half Waiaria Ellis sliced open the Black Ferns defensive line for a try in the 67th minute.

That was the start of a bright spot for the Wallaroos, who produced a driving maul from close range, with reserve hooker Brittany Merlo scoring Australia's third try.

World.title: Third woman engages lawyer over 'incredibly traumatic' Sydney Swans scandal
World.content:
A lawyer representing a third woman involved in the Sydney Swans sexual assault scandal says a potential civil lawsuit is being looked at.

Slater and Gordon senior lawyer, Jackson Pannam, has been engaged to represent a woman who he said contacted police immediately following the alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne in the early hours of Monday, August 17.

"Our client has had her entire world turned upside down and is now trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience," he said.

He said the firm's lawyers "see the profound and long-lasting impact that serious injury, loss and abuse can have on people's lives".

Jackson Pannam says the woman's world has been "turned upside down" by the incident. (ABC News)

On Friday, Carbone Lawyers announced separately that it was representing two women, believed to be adult entertainers involved in the incident, and looking into launching a civil claim.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at the Pullman Hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' victory against Essendon last Sunday night.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following the match in Melbourne.

Mr Pannam said following her initial contact with police, his client was continuing to speak to them as part of their investigation into the incident.

"Everyone deserves to be safe going about their life, at home, at work, and in public spaces without risk of being assaulted or harmed," Mr Pannam said.

"We're standing with our client to give her support at this difficult time, and to help her get the justice she deserves."

Mr Pannam described the woman as "extremely distressed" by what had occurred, and asked for her privacy, and that of the other women involved, to be respected.

He said his client had not spoken to the media.

A police investigation is still underway, but they have not made any arrests or laid charges.

On Saturday, police provided an update about the investigation being undertaken by detectives from the Sexual Crimes Squad.

"The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established, and a number of people have been spoken to," the statement read.

"As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further, including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken."

In a statement, the Sydney Swans said the club "supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today's statement regarding the investigation".

The club's statement also addressed comments relating to other men, beyond the five players identified by the club, being present in the hotel room at the centre of the allegations.

"The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation," it read.

"The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage."

World.title: Late collapse sees Australia surrender commanding position on day one in Mackay
World.content:
A stunning middle-order collapse has seen Australia surrender a commanding position on day one of the second Test in Mackay.

Towering quick Shoriful Islam, playing his first Test in Australia, took six wickets to rival a sensational new-ball spell from Mitchell Starc earlier in the day, with the two left-armers combining for 12 of the day's 18 wickets.

Cam Green, off the back of a drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again the only Australian batter to stand tall, guiding his side to a score of 8-165 and a 101-run lead at stumps on the first day of cricket to be played at Australia's newest Test venue.

If the afternoon and evening belonged to Bangladesh, the morning belonged to Mitch Starc.

The veteran spearhead took six wickets, five of them in a single, devastating opening spell, to deliver what looked to be the perfect response for Australia, still stinging from its shock defeat in Darwin.

Bangladesh, blitzed out for just 64 off the back off Starc's tremendous 6-12, were brought crashing back down to Earth with an unceremonious thud.

Starc struck with his very first ball and, 22 deliveries later, had a five wicket haul in a brutal passage of play that saw him take 5-5 in his six-over spell.

Mitchell Starc claimed a first ball wicket in both of this first two overs. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Shadman Islam, Tanzid Hasan, Najmul Hossain Shanto and Litton Das were all dismissed for ducks, while Mominul Haque managed just 9 as the tourists fell to 5-12 inside seven overs after loosing the toss and being asked to bat.

Pat Cummins (3-25) and Josh Hazlewood (1-18) also got in on the act, before Starc returned to claim the wicket of number 11 batter Shoriful Islam for 14, Bangladesh's top scorer on a chastening morning of cricket.

Bangladesh's score of 64 was the fourth-lowest Test total in their history and a return to normality as far as Australia were concerned.

In reply though, Australia was unconvincing to begin, then meek and brittle as shadows lengthened in Mackay.

Matt Renshaw was caught at slip off a leading edge for 8, and Travis Head chopped on for 22 to leave the Aussies 2-40.

Renshaw was dimissed cheaply on his return to the Test arena. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Head fell to Shoriful's second ball of the match, and later that same over he had another wicket to his name, the hapless Marnus Labuschagne bowled off his thigh pad for just 4 runs.

The conversation over the Queensland number three was already a clamour, and should Labuschagne fail in the second innings — if required — they could prove impossible to ignore ahead of a tough three-Test series in South Africa next month.

Smith and Green came together either side of tea to build Australia's lead with a 77-run partnership.

Smith was a touch unfortunate to be given out LBW on 42 to Shoriful, given out by umpire Kumar Dharmasena on field, with DRS showing the ball would have brushed the off stump to maintain the on field decision.

Alex Carey, playing his 50th Test and becoming just the seventh Australian to do so, came and went quickly, mistiming his slog and being caught in the deep for 5.

Shoriful proceeded to tear through the Australian lower order, dismissing Beau Webster LBW for a first-ball duck, having Cummins caught for a second-ball duck and then Starc bowled for 1.

Green ended the day on 51, with Nathan Lyon alongside him as Bangladesh clung onto the hosts' coat tails in this series.

Relive all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: Lions coach 'feels sorry' for Swans as likely finals clash looms
World.content:
Embattled Sydney will brace for further fallout from the scandal that has rocked the AFL club, while finalising preparations for a dead rubber against North Melbourne on Sunday.

On Thursday, five players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon — were suspended for the rest of the season for "breaching club standards".

Separately, a police investigation continues into the events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

On Friday, coach Dean Cox distanced himself from any blame for the events at the hotel, while captain Callum Mills said "we believe that the five players have let us down".

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham on Wednesday said the club-imposed sanctions would "torpedo" the second-placed Swans' premiership hopes.

Swans coach Dean Cox (left) and captain Callum Mills spoke to reporters on Friday. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

In their SCG qualifying final, Sydney will most likely face reigning premiers Brisbane, who all but locked in third place with Friday night's 63-point win over Collingwood, unless Hawthorn leapfrog them on percentage with a big win over West Coast.

The team that finishes fourth plays runaway minor premiers Fremantle while third faces a decimated and embattled Sydney.

"I don't mind either or, to be honest with you," Lions coach Chris Fagan said after Friday night's match.

"It's just good to get the double chance.

"And I'm sort of thinking that Sydney have lost some players obviously due to the unfortunate thing that happened last week. But in some ways that can galvanise a club too.

"The guys that do get to play just might go that much harder and be that much more difficult to beat.

"So either way I'm just happy we finished top four. We travel well. Either way we're going to have to travel, so we'll take whatever comes our way."

McKenna, Morris magic lifts Lions to vital big win over Pies Brisbane Lions put the foot down against Collingwood, with magic from Conor McKenna and Logan Morris seeing the premiers take a strong grip on third spot.

Fagan hasn't spoken to his players specifically about the Sydney situation.

"There's been so much publicity around it — it almost goes without saying," Fagan said.

"I don't feel like I need to have a conversation with my players because it's pretty obvious, the repercussions for not thinking through your actions too clearly. And yeah, it's really unfortunate.

"I do feel sorry for Sydney because they have been such a terrific club in that regard for a long, long time but these sorts of things happen. It's just a bit of a head-scratcher, isn't it?

"You just wonder what was going through people's heads to let that occur."

Sydney on Friday disputed assertions there were more than five players in the East Melbourne hotel room on Monday morning.

James Rowbottom, Harry Cunningham, Angus Sheldrick, Caiden Cleary and Tom Hanily will replace the banned five players for the North Melbourne clash.

That game takes place after Sydney's AFLW clash with Essendon as part of a double header.

World.title: Argentina star hit with one of the biggest bans in World Cup history
World.content:
FIFA banned three Argentina players overnight, including a 10-match suspension for midfielder Leandro Paredes, for striking Spain opponents after losing the World Cup final.

The ban for Paredes — who grabbed Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat and pushed Gavi to the ground — ranks with the FIFA sanctions for Uruguay forward Luis Suárez in 2014 as among the most severe in World Cup history.

Argentina defender Nahuel Molina was handed a seven-game ban while Thiago Almada was given a one-game suspension. FIFA imposed fines of $US90,000 ($AU125,000) on Paredes and Molina, and $US30,000 for Almada.

The ban for Paredes is effectively a one-year expulsion from the Argentina team as the FIFA calendar for national team schedules includes 10 games through June 2027.

All of those games could be friendlies with no competitive games currently scheduled.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina is confronted by Spanish captain Rodri after the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Martin Rickett/PA Images)

Gavi also was banned for one game, which is a Nations League match for Spain against England at Wembley on September 26.

An Argentina coach, Roberto Ayala, was also handed a three-game ban and a $US30,000 fine.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) was fined $US110,000 for a range of incidents during the World Cup, including players carrying a political banner about the Falkland Islands after the semifinal win against England, and discriminatory chants by fans.

AFA was also ordered by FIFA to spend $US100,000 on anti-racism projects. Argentina received $US34 million in World Cup prize money from FIFA.

AFA can appeal the longer sanctions and fines to FIFA, and likely after at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

"The AFA legal department will, in a timely manner, request from FIFA the grounds for the reviewable rulings in order to file appeals with the governing body's appeal committee, while retaining the future option of appealing to the CAS as a final recourse," the federation said in a statement.

Luis Suárez holds his teeth after biting Italy's Giorgio Chiellini. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

In 2014, Suárez was banned from all soccer for four months, including for his new club Barcelona, and eight more competition games for Uruguay for biting Italian defender Giorgio Chiellini in a World Cup group stage game in Brazil.

Paredes' 10-game ban equals that in 2013 for Josip Simunic of Croatia after winning a World Cup qualifying play-off. Simunic used a megaphone to lead fans chanting a slogan used by the country's pro-Nazi regime during World War II.

The on-field clashes at last month's final in East Rutherford, New Jersey — which were charged by FIFA as assault cases — came after Argentina lost a testy final to Spain where the team was mostly outplayed and barely created a scoring chance.

Spain forward Ferran Torres scored the only goal in the second period of extra time, after Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off.

FIFA disciplinary judges also ordered Argentina to play its next home game in a stadium limited to 50 per cent of capacity. FIFA deferred a second stadium sanction and a $US100,000 fine for probationary periods.

World.title: Wildcard woes: Why the Crows are walking a tightrope
World.content:
The weight of expectation can be a relentless burden.

For a success starved fanbase it can fuel volatility and in a two-team town it's a pressure cooker.

On the eve of finals, the Adelaide Crows find themselves walking a wildcard tightrope.

If the Lions, Hawks, Demons or Cats fail to lose their final round match-ups, which they are heavily favoured to win, the Crows would have to face Carlton or the Western Bulldogs in a sudden death showdown that 12 months ago didn't even exist.

Since the AFL expanded to 18 sides, a 15-win season guaranteed you a Top 6 finish in 11 of the 13 full length seasons and only twice locked in an away elimination final.

Now even if Adelaide beats GWS on Saturday night, it could still face the precarious possibility of being both the first minor premier in the AFL to exit in straight sets and the first ever side to lose a wildcard final.

It's a situation that will only amplify an emotional fanbase that is losing faith in its game plan and direction; often questioning selection and coaching online after results.

Adelaide's success starved fanbase make their opinions known. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Adelaide Head of Football Adam Kelly addressed their behaviour a month ago on SA Grandstand stating their performances were being exaggerated.

"Our game certainly stacks up. We've had some terrific wins and some disappointing losses but there are very few teams who don't have that," he said.

" Adelaide is a very noisy place. We just need to make sure we stay focused on what's important and stay grounded and realistic about where our game is at. "

Some pundits, including 4x Showdown Medallist Josh Francou, feel anything less than a preliminary final appearance would be a failed season.

"Based on last year and the list they've got, if I'm an Adelaide supporter and I'm not playing in a preliminary final that's a fail to me. You can't win a premiership from a wildcard," he said.

"I still have a lot of question marks over Adelaide. I can't work out what's happening off field with selection and they're the number one pressure team but when sides apply pressure to them they can't handle it."

Adelaide's AFL finals drought is over With a cohesive and suffocating defence, the Adelaide Crows have the tools to put the ghosts of 2017 behind them and reach the top of the AFL mountain.

Meanwhile, others believe a strong season doesn't always lead into another. Premiership winning Crow Rod Jameson foreshadowed this after Adelaide's qualifying final loss to Collingwood last year.

"It doesn't guarantee you'll play finals again next year. If they get a couple of key injuries and drop the odd game, they'll be under enormous pressure," he predicted.

The reality is winning a minor premiership guarantees nothing but a coin flip. Only 54 per cent of winners in the AFL era have gone on to secure a premiership within three years.

Is Nicks the man?

Unfortunately Crows fans are conditioned to a ruthless pursuit of success with Matthew Nicks the first coach in their history to survive three seasons without finals.

In the past, the club has been swift in its desire to bring a fresh voice in when momentum dwindled. Now it's headstrong in its pursuit of culture and firm in its belief Nicks is their man, extending him until the end of 2027 in December.

Matthew Nicks (left) has been Adelaide's coach since 2019. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Crows president John Olsen told ABC Sport ahead of their Round 13 clash with Geelong that the club was close to breaking its near 30-year drought.

"We are united in the view that we are nearly there," he said.

"We accept we have to take it up another gear with consistency but we're not far off the pace."

"Over my six years at the club I've seen impatient fans … sustained success is what every club wants to achieve. That means you have to be deliberate, focused and disciplined in how you go about attracting talent to the club."

Selection on the ground

Adelaide's underwhelming campaign can be attributed to numerous factors.

Availability of star players was a huge problem in the first half of the season.

Izak Rankine's pre-season hamstring issue and suspension meant the man who is currently the highest ranked player in the league over the last five rounds took eight weeks to be unleashed into the midfield.

Their three-time winning best and fairest winner and skipper Jordan Dawson had to take personal leave after the tragic passing of his brother.

Crows captain Jordan Dawson had to miss several matches this year. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

All-Australian forward Riley Thilthorpe's output has dropped after tweaking his back travelling to Perth whilst Darcy Fogarty's own back issue saw him miss several weeks and key defender Mark Keane's broken ankle left the side without their defensive talisman until Round 15.

Despite the adversities, honourable losses to league heavyweights created optimism that once the troops were back the Crows would rise again.

To a degree they have, winning 8 of 11 games after their bye; but questions remain over their game plan and its ability to take the club to the top of the mountain.

The introduction and reshaping of numerous rules in the off season were designed to encourage free-flowing brands of footy.

Forever a Crow, Taylor Walker remains the boy from Broken Hill Taylor Walker arrived at the Adelaide Football Club as a 75-kilogram prospect who had only ever wanted to be a footballer. More than 300 AFL games and 700 goals later, he will retire as a club great.

Most have adopted that mantra with the ladder leading Fremantle Dockers giving Adelaide a harsh lesson last Friday on ball movement ending with +248 handball metres gained and 64 per cent ball use rating to the Crows 40 per cent.

It's a common theme for Adelaide who are last in the league for handball metres gained and third last for D50 to F50 transition.

It's a style that can open you up to immense pressure leading to high turnover rates in dangerous areas with the Crows 18th for defensive half turnovers.

The positive is they've improved on last year's midfield weakness, rising from 18th in clearance differential in the final month of 2025 to 7th in 2026 and are 4th across the season for score from centre bounce differential.

The other issue facing the Crows is selection. Their use of the new fifth bench rotation is puzzling with Matthew Nicks often prioritising pinch hit ruckman Toby Murray with limited impact.

Murray is second last for time on ground percentage (54 per cent) for players who've featured over 10 times. This decision came to a head last round when Murray had just two touches in 66 minutes.

Fans will farewell Taylor Walker at the Crows v GWS match on Saturday. (AAP: Matt Turner)

Meanwhile the management of retiring veteran Taylor Walker is in the spotlight after being flown to Perth but not selected for the finals shaping clash as a result of the clubs third game in 12 days; when the team faced cellar dwellers Richmond the week prior and could've rested their 36-year-old then.

It was an issue back in May when he played against Brisbane at the Gabba and then tore his hamstring in the Showdown five days later.

The AFL has openly said wildcard wins will be treated as a finals victory; news that was music to the ears of Essendon supporters who haven't won a final in over 8,000 days.

If Adelaide wins a match-up against a 10th placed side next weekend it might be a relief inside the four walls at West Lakes but will it satisfy a rabid fanbase?

We'll find out in a week's time.

You can hear ABC Sport's call of Adelaide v GWS from 7pm CST on ABC Listen and 891 ABC Adelaide.

World.title: 'Sad and disappointed' Sinner to miss first Grand Slam in seven years
World.content:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open, unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning his Wimbledon title.

Sinner beat Alexander Zverev last month for his second straight title at the All England Club, but then pulled out of the hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

The 25-year-old Italian wrote Friday that he will not be ready when the main draw begins on August 30.

"Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year," Sinner wrote in a post on X.

"We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue. I'm obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there."

Sinner was the 2024 US Open champion and lost to Carlos Alcaraz in last year's final.

Alcaraz posted on social media on Thursday that he would be ready to play in New York after being out of action since April because of a right wrist injury.

The rivalry between the two has dominated men's tennis in recent years, and they met in the past three Grand Slam finals in 2025. Alcaraz took the most recent one with his four-set victory in New York.

That ended Sinner's title reign after he beat Taylor Fritz in straight sets in the 2024 final.

Sinner is 44-3 with six titles this year. He had a stunning collapse at the French Open, blowing a two-set lead while struggling in the heat in his second-round match against Juan Manuel Cerundolo.

He then sat out until Wimbledon, where his victory gave him five Grand Slam titles.

It will be the first time Sinner has missed a Grand Slam tournament since making his major debut at the US Open in 2019.

Tech.title: HoverAir’s transforming modular drone has already been halted in the US
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US

I am so sorry, fellow US gadget fans: the FCC’s drone ban appears to have struck again. The HoverAir Versa — a baby steadycam with snap-on propeller wings that transform it into a drone — has already stopped taking US orders just three days after its Indiegogo debut, and may be forced to abandon shipping plans in the US.

HoverAir is now telling backers it’s only shipping its camera to the US, not the piece that turns it into a drone, “due to a few remaining logistics updates with the Flight Kit.” But those “logistics” may actually be a euphemism for “we’ve been banned by the federal government.” The FCC’s database no longer has an entry for the HoverAir Versa at all, suggesting that its authorization grant has been pulled.

Image: Indiegogo

On Wednesday, I told you how giving a camera wings probably wasn’t a good enough loophole to keep the FCC from feeling tricked. Even though the HoverAir Versa did make it through the FCC on August 9th, we confirmed, that approval was for a camera, not a drone. The Chinese company, Zero Zero Robotics, told the FCC’s agent the camera shouldn’t be blocked because Zero Zero isn’t on the FCC’s Covered List for cameras — which is true.

But all companies are automatically on the FCC’s covered list for drones and critical drone components, and the FCC explicitly defines cameras as one of those components.

Early buyers may need refunds. Image: Indiegogo

If HoverAir’s camera authorization is now rejected, it won’t just be the “Flight Kit” accessory that it can’t import, market, or sell in the United States. The camera portion won’t be legal, either, as it needs FCC authorization too.

Currently, HoverAir’s Indiegogo page no longer shows the “Flight Kit” as a selectable option to people browsing from the US, but it does still market it, and backers can order the camera portion. When I use a VPN to change my internet address to Canada, combos that include the Flight Kit suddenly appear.

That won’t help US residents buy one, though. In the Indiegogo comments section, one backer who already ordered the camera wrote: “When looking at my pledge, it shows that they can’t ship to my address.”

These are the only options now available to backers in the US, and even they may disappear. Image: Indiegogo

HoverAir did not immediately respond to a request for comment. We’ve asked the company whether it will commit to refunds more quickly this time around — when the brand failed to obtain certification for the waterproof HoverAir Aqua last December, it spent months telling backers it would ship as soon as possible rather than revealing the truth.

I tried to speak to the FCC about what’s going on, but once again, an agency spokesperson refused to go on the record.

Tech.title: TikTok will pay $400 million to settle DOJ child privacy lawsuit
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US Department of Justice announced on Friday that TikTok will pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit filed in 2024 over allegedly violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). In the lawsuit, the DOJ alleged that TikTok collected data from children without notifying parents or obtaining consent and did not delete the accounts when parents requested.

TikTok is set to pay $300 million right away and will pay a further $100 million “upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly,” the DOJ says in a press release. The settlement is “one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a COPPA case.”

The DOJ also notes that TikTok has “undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices” since the lawsuit was filed and that TikTok has “implemented extensive measures designed to strengthen safeguards for younger users, improve age-related controls, and enhance parental oversight.”

TikTok didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. In January, the deal to put TikTok under a new joint ownership structure in the US finally happened.

Tech.title: Over 1 million people have clicked LinkedIn’s AI slop button
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

LinkedIn actually announced a “Seems like AI slop” button on July 30th, and the company says that a lot of people have already used it. According to a Thursday post from chief product officer Hari Srinivasan, “over a million people” have clicked on the button, which is accessible from the three dots menu on a post.

LinkedIn announced the button a few weeks after AI detector Pangram determined that 41 percent of LinkedIn’s longform posts were flagged as fully AI generated, which 404 Media reported on. Alongside the AI slop button, LinkedIn introduced “new and improved” classifiers to identify posts as AI and removed a feature that would “enhance your post” with AI.

“AI slop is a top priority for all of us,” Srinivasan said at the time, and it sounds as if the platform’s changes may be making a difference. In Thursday’s post, Srinivasan said that users are overall “now experiencing 40% less views on what we classify as AI slop from just a few weeks ago.”

LinkedIn is also adding a new message that will tell users who make a post if “Some members told us this post seems like AI.”

“We approached this assuming good intent; I know I’m increasingly conscious on how to not sound like AI & the goal is to provide helpful feedback,” Srinivasan said.

Image: LinkedIn

Earlier this year, LinkedIn also said it would be cracking down on comments users create at scale “with little or no human involvement.”

Tech.title: Apple is laying off staffers working on the Vision Pro and Siri
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is laying off staff on the Siri and the Vision Pro teams, according to Bloomberg. The cuts include “largely shutting down” a Vision Pro gaming team and “reducing the size” of the team that makes Vision Pro immersive content, the publication says. More than 200 jobs were cut.

Apple said in a statement to Bloomberg it was making the changes to “to evolve our business to deliver the best experiences for our users,” though it will be making new roles. The company didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge.

The Vision Pro launched in early 2024 as Apple’s big bet on “spatial computing,” but the $3,499 headset doesn’t appear to have been a big hit. While Bloomberg reported in May that Apple is working on “a slimmer and lighter headset” to succeed the current Vision Pro (which was updated last year with an M5 chip), a report a few weeks after said that Apple was suspending work with Samsung Display on a display for an entry-level XR machine.

However, following the success of Meta’s smart glasses, Apple is apparently planning to make its own smart glasses, with Bloomberg reporting recently that Apple plans to announce them at WWDC (typically a June event) in 2027 and launch them by the end of that year.

The company finally launched its revamped, AI-powered Siri at this year’s WWDC. The new Siri is set to be available to the public in beta later this year.

Tech.title: $100 Best Buy gift cards will be $60 at stores Saturday
Tech.content:
The best gift card deal we’ve spotted this year is happening Saturday, August 22nd, at Best Buy stores for one day only. In celebration of the retailer’s 60th anniversary, you can purchase a $100 Best Buy gift card for $60. The deal is only good for as long as supplies last at your local store, so you might want to plan on getting there no later than opening time to boost your chance of getting one.

There are some limitations on how you can use the gift card. You can’t use them to buy other gift cards, like iTunes or Google Play credit, and they also can’t be used to buy prepaid or open-loop debit cards. However, they can be used in combination with other discounts or promotions on products from Best Buy, and any returns or cancellations you make will credit back to the gift card.

We’ve found a number of deals during Best Buy’s 60th anniversary sale that you can apply that gift card to. The iPad Air M4 dropped to $649, the lowest we’ve seen since the prices went up this summer, and the AirPods Max 2 are only $429, $120 lower than their usual price. There are a variety of discounts on Windows and macOS laptops too, like this HP OmniBook X Flip 2-in-1 for $749.99, a $450 discount from the typical price.

Tech.title: Walmart is finally adding Apple Pay and Google Pay
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Walmart will soon allow you to pay for your items with Google Pay or Apple Pay. In an announcement on Friday, Walmart says it’s going to bring tap-to-pay capabilities to “select” Walmart and Sam’s Club locations starting August 24th, before rolling out support to all US stores by the end of 2026 and gas stations by mid-2027.

This launch has been a long time coming, as Walmart was one of the last major retailers not to support Apple Pay or Google Pay. The retail giant even backed the launch of the short-lived CurrentC mobile payment service before rolling out Walmart Pay in 2016, which lets you quickly check out with a QR code at its stores. A Walmart spokesperson doubled down on its decision not to support NFC-based payments in a statement to MacRumors last year, saying the company offers “convenient solutions” like Walmart Pay instead. But now, the company seems to have changed its tune.

“We want customers and members to have choice in how they pay, so they can check out in the way that works best for them,” Walmart’s announcement says. “Tap to Pay is a great addition to the other payment options already offered like cash, credit card or Walmart Pay.”

Tech.title: Microsoft and Discord subpoenaed over GTA VI gameplay leaks
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series

Following several apparent video leaks of Grand Theft Auto VI, Take-Two Interactive has subpoenaed Microsoft and Discord over content that “infringes copyrights” held for the game, Kotaku reports. In the subpoenas, filed on Thursday, Take-Two says copyrighted material includes “audiovisual content, artwork, images, dialogue, or other creative elements” and it is looking to identify “alleged infringers at issue.” The subpoenas give Microsoft and Discord until September 4th to produce the requested information.

The leaked clips have been watermarked by a person or group going by “CyberLeek,” and they have shown what appears to be GTA VI protagonist Jason Duval (one of two protagonists) doing various activities, including driving, flying an airplane, using a taser, and attacking somebody with a wrench. In one clip, the player spells “LEEK” by shooting holes in a wall.

Discord and Microsoft didn’t immediately reply to requests for comment. On X, Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet says that “We are working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support efforts to protect creative works and intellectual property.”

The leaks have popped up ahead of Rockstar’s big extended preview of the game that is set to debut on Netflix on August 27th. The full game is scheduled to launch on November 19th.

Update, August 21st: Added statement from Xbox’s CTO.

Tech.title: Pixel 11 gets in on the digicam trend
Tech.content:
I recently looked back at a photo I’d taken on a smartphone in 2014, and I was struck by just how good it looked. The details were soft, the shadows were dark. It was the kind of photo I felt like I hadn’t seen out of a phone in years. That might be changing, though. The Pixel 11 includes a suite of new photography features called Camera Looks that allow those who really care about those things (hi, it’s all of us) to dial in their preferences and get rid of that modern over-processed look.

On today’s episode of The Vergecast, David Imel joins us to discuss his time reviewing the Pixel 11 Pro and how he’s thinking about its new approach to computational photography. After that, we’ve got a super-sized edition of Brendan Carr is a Dummy, everyone’s favorite podcast with a podcast. It was a big week for bad telecom policy, and we’re giving it the time it deserves. Tech.title: Michael Polansky is training an AI model on skin that’s still alive
Tech.content:
Michael Polansky is remarkably unassuming for someone operating in a corner of the world known for outsize egos.

Seated at a leafy patio outside a popular bakery in Mill Valley, an affluent town about 15 miles north of San Francisco, Polansky — bespectacled, his fresh face framed by dark hair shot through with gray — has the look and the friendly demeanor of a young professor.

He is, in fact, both the co-founder of a buzzy AI and biology startup called Outer Biosciences and the creative, business, and romantic partner to Stefani Germanotta — better known as Lady Gaga. It’s an unlikely double life. On the one hand, the couple invariably moves in the world that comes with celebrity; on the other, he’s running an outfit that has spent years figuring out how to keep living human tissue alive outside the body — for over a month, so far — without anyone outside the company knowing.

He didn’t see any of it coming. Polansky grew up in Minnesota and went on to Harvard, where he studied applied mathematics and computer science, graduating in 2006. Afterward, he logged three years at the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates — “a very unique place,” Polansky says over coffee, and one where he had “a really good experience,” even if it wasn’t a place he was going to “wake up and be excited about . . .every day.”

His pilgrimage from Bridgewater to Silicon Valley ran through Minnesota. By coincidence, Sean Parker’s assistant at the time had been Polansky’s neighbor growing up. At a 2009 wedding in their home state, she mentioned that Parker was looking for someone to work with him. Polansky already knew who Parker was and was looking to move west. The two had dinner in New York, “hit it off immediately,” and, as Polansky tells it, he quit Bridgewater the next day and moved to San Francisco.

He first landed a role as a principal at Founders Fund when the firm was run by its four original partners — Peter Thiel, Sean Parker, Luke Nosek and Ken Howery – with Polansky and another young principal at the time, Brian Singerman, sharing an office. “It was a really, really great experience,” Polansky says.

When Parker left Founders Fund after becoming liquid in his Facebook stock and wanted to build out his own family office, he brought Polansky with him. Polansky ran that office — handling Parker’s business, investment, and philanthropic interests, including helping stand up the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy (where Polansky remains executive director) until COVID, when his life “moved in a different direction.”

That change had a lot to do with Germanotta. Polansky met her in late 2019 at one of Parker’s birthday parties. Charmingly, the meeting came at the urging of her mother, Cynthia Germanotta, president of the Born This Way Foundation, whom Polansky had come to know through his philanthropic work.

“She had said, you know, for months and months, ‘I want to set you up with my daughter,’” Polansky recalls. “I was like, I think you’re making fun of me.” She wasn’t. When their own mothers later met, he says, laughing, “it all made perfect sense.” (His mother and Germanotta’s mother are now close friends.)

Their relationship is a full partnership, professionally and personally. Notably, for Gaga’s most recent world tour, which began in July of last year and ended in April, the couple managed a massive operation across three 747s, something Polansky compares to running “a 200-person startup that travels around the world every day.”

It also includes Haus Labs, the cosmetics brand Germanotta initially built “on her kitchen floor,” Polansky says, instead of simply licensing her name to an existing company. That business, based in El Segundo, California, an operation with roughly 70 employees, is reportedly thriving.

Germanotta also sits on the board of Outer Biosciences, and the two companies collaborate at the margins. For example, Outer Biosciences’ chief scientist, Kyung-Jin Jang, sits on Haus Labs’ scientific advisory board, and the companies have run some joint projects.

Says Polansky, beaming as he talks about her from our sun-dappled table: “People really haven’t gotten to know a certain side of her publicly … She’s such a brilliant businessperson.”

From cancer to tissue in a dish

While Polansky is also a businessperson, he’s not a scientist. He got into life sciences “accidentally,” he says, through more than a decade spent alongside Parker in cancer immunotherapy, a field that was “very fringe” when they entered it.

Outer Biosciences, co-founded in 2022 by Polansky (CEO), Jang, Chris Hinojosa (CTO), and Stanley King (chief business officer), grew out of frustration that the pace of innovation in biology and chemistry has never matched software, in large part because there’s no ethical way to run experiments directly on people. Meanwhile, the proxies scientists rely on instead — animal models, simplified cell cultures, lab-grown organoids — are poor stand-ins for how a real human organ behaves.

So Outer Biosciences took a different approach. Instead of engineering a synthetic organ, the company sources human skin that would otherwise be discarded after surgery – mostly plastic surgery – through what it describes as vetted non-profit and commercial biobanks and brokers operating under “institutional review board oversight and documented donor consent,” principally the National Disease Research Interchange and the Cooperative Human Tissue Network. (Both outfits receive federal funding from the NIH and the National Cancer Institute without being federally operated.)

Polansky is careful to note that there is no single government tissue network that qualifies buyers. He says Outer Biosciences pays fees to these suppliers on a cost-recovery basis rather than purchasing tissue outright. He also says the company spent roughly two years on building that pipeline and handling the protocols required to receive that tissue “within hours” of surgery, while it’s still living.

Asked about the donors’ privacy, he says that every sample arrives already de-identified — stripped upstream by the supplying organizations of names, contact information and other direct identifiers. A proprietary support system developed by his team then feeds the tissue nutrients and removes metabolic waste, extending its viable life well past the industry norm.

That norm, by the way, is a matter of days. That’s enough time to test for acute toxicity, but not for slower biological processes like collagen remodeling, pigmentation change, or barrier repair that take weeks to unfold. (Dermatologists routinely tell patients to expect changes over a matter of weeks for this same reason.)

Outer Biosciences’ system meanwhile keeps tissue alive for up to a month, says Polansky, who says it retains its “day-zero architecture and preserves its day-zero epidermal, stromal and immune-associated molecular programs.” In plainer English, that means that 30-day-old tissue cared for by the company looks a lot like day-one tissue, but it isn’t fully indistinguishable from it.

Sunburn is one of the clearer examples of what that extra time buys Outer Biosciences. Polansky says that its researchers can induce UVB damage in living tissue, then track the stress, inflammatory, and recovery-related responses that follow over the following weeks as an information-gathering exercise. He says the team isn’t “healing” the skin but rather watching an injury happen and then watching the biology that follows it over time.

Perhaps anticipating pushback from the scientific community, Polansky is careful about how he frames the company’s achievements when this reporter asks questions about rival technologies. The startup’s value, he says, isn’t any one piece of what it’s doing but how the pieces fit together: human tissue that can be kept alive for weeks, a diverse donor pool that Outer Biosciences’ team can subject to controlled experimental conditions, and repeated molecular measurements taken along the way.

And it’s all fed into one, closed self-enforcing system. An AI model predicts which untested chemicals are likely to have a beneficial effect on a specific skin function. Those chemicals get run through the living-tissue system. Then the results, whether the prediction was right or wrong, get fed back into the model, improving the next round of guesses.

It’s a giant improvement from where things started, says Polansky. Early on, the company relied on a “brute force” approach, mining scientific literature and partnering with the National Cancer Institute on natural compounds from extreme environments. That phase produced a couple of leads over about 18 months, but with AI layered in, the company is now generating a new candidate roughly every six weeks, with six leads currently active in its pipeline and several dozen additional “hits” logged.

What makes that pace truly astonishing, Polansky says as the crowd around us thins out, is the size of the current universe of skin-active ingredients.

It’s almost impossible to know the exact number, but it’s small. “Active ingredient” means something different informally than it does formally. While the FDA maintains rules covering 13 categories of over-the-counter skin drugs (think sunscreen, antifungals), across all of them, only about 120 to 130 active ingredients are approved. Add cosmetic ingredients backed by actual research, says Polansky, and that number is closer to 200.

This, of course, presents opportunities.

Outer Biosciences is discovering cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, so there’s no FDA approval to seek out. Instead, the route runs through two steps: first, getting the ingredient a standardized industry name; then safety testing under guidelines set by the OECD, a Paris-based international body whose member countries agree to accept each other’s properly run studies — meaning a study done correctly in one participating country is accepted in the other 40-plus.

A partner outfit then commercializes the whole thing. Indeed, rather than build its own consumer brand, Outer Biosciences right now plans to license or sell its finished ingredients to beauty or pharma outfits that will then formulate these into actual products (a serum, a cream) and bring them to market under their own brands. Already, four of Outer Biosciences’ six current leads look likely to reach commercialization, Polansky says.

In the meantime, the company is generating money from collaborative research partnerships, including a pharmaceutical partner that’s studying why certain cancer drugs cause severe skin rashes, and consumer beauty brands that are testing whether Outer Biosciences’ data holds up against their own product-development and marketing needs.
